activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
Rebecca would tell you, if you asked, that she had cooked dinner plenty of times before, but this was not entirely true. There had been pasta with jarred sauce, and toast, and one ambitious night of scrambled eggs. Tonight, though, her mother was working the late shift at the hospital and had left a whole raw chicken in the refrigerator with a note that said only, oven 375. Rebecca had volunteered, and she was not sure now whether she had volunteered out of love or out of a wish to be the kind of daughter who volunteered.

She was at the grocery store first because the recipe Emersyn had sent her called for lemons and thyme, and because she wanted twenty minutes alone with a cart. Antony was working the register, and he waved her over even though his line was four customers deep.

"You're buying a whole chicken," he said. "Again. Did you not already have one?"

"This is for lemons. And thyme. And, fine, I'll admit it, I don't actually know what a shallot is."

"That's an onion with ambition." He scanned the lemons slowly, as if granting her more time by doing so. "My mom used to rinse the chicken in the sink first. Every time. I did it too until like, last year."

Rebecca paid and said she'd see him Monday, and in the parking lot she thought about her grandmother, who had washed chicken under running water with the seriousness of ritual, who had taught Rebecca's mother, who had probably taught nobody anything because she ordered takeout. At home she took the chicken from its wrapping, held it over the sink, and turned the tap.

Her younger brother appeared in the doorway in his socks. "Stop. You can't wash it."

"I'm not washing it. I'm rinsing it." This distinction felt important for about two seconds.

"Emersyn told me the CDC says not to wash raw chicken," he said. "The water splashes and it spreads bacteria to the sink and everything near it. She did a whole presentation on it." He leaned against the counter, insufferable and possibly correct. "Did you splash yet?"

Rebecca turned off the tap. The chicken sat there, pale and cold in her hands, and she had a visceral sense of all the invisible things that might already be on the counter, the cutting board, her sleeves. It was not a comfortable feeling. It was also, she suspected, mostly imaginary, which somehow made it worse, because she couldn't see where the true danger ended and her own squeamishness began.

"You could just, like, wipe everything down," her brother offered. He had a way of offering wisdom as though it were a platitude he'd picked up somewhere and was testing for authenticity. "Or you could text Emersyn and apologize for making fun of her presentation."

"I never made fun of her presentation."

"You said it was about a chicken."

"It was about a chicken." She set the bird in the roasting pan and washed her hands for a long time, longer than seemed reasonable, and no one was there to absolve her of the excess. Her grandmother had been a careful woman, careful in the old way, the way of vinegar and boiling water and faith in running taps. Rebecca understood, holding the lemon over the chicken, that her grandmother's care and the CDC's care were not opposites so much as two answers to the same fear, one inherited and one researched, and that she was standing in the kitchen where they'd just collided. She could not prove which was truer. She only knew which one she could verify, and that verification felt like a smaller kind of love.

She salted the skin and tucked thyme under it, and the chicken went into the oven at 375, exactly as the note said. While it roasted she wiped down the counter twice, then the sink, then the counter again, and her brother watched from the stool without saying anything else, which she chose to interpret as respect.

When her mother came home at ten, smelling of hand sanitizer and fluorescent light, dinner was warm under foil and the kitchen was spotlessly, almost suspiciously clean. Her mother lifted the foil, said "You didn't wash it, did you," and Rebecca, slicing through the crisp skin, answered, "No. But I wiped everything down twice, and I need you to not ask why."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
Lucas had chosen cooking class because his schedule had a hole in it, not because he wanted to cook. He stood at the steel counter in room 114, holding a palette knife over a slab of dark chocolate, while Ms. Campbell read out temperatures from the front. Forty-five degrees to melt, twenty-seven to cool, thirty-one to work. He had written the numbers on his wrist in pen, where the chocolate would not smear them.

Their assignment was a tray of moulded shells, due out of the fridge before the bell. Tye worked two stations down, humming, patient with everything, patient in a way that Lucas found useful and faintly annoying. Tye had scraped his bowl the way the handout said, dragged the spatula through the melted chocolate over and over until it thickened, but Lucas had skipped most of that. Stirring took time, and time was the thing he had least of, and the chocolate looked the same at the end whether he stirred it or not. That was his reasoning and he kept it to himself. He filled his mould with a steady hand, tapped out the bubbles, and slid it onto the shelf beside Tye's.

The subtext of the next ten minutes was lost on Lucas until later. Tye kept glancing at the shelf, at Lucas's mould, then away. "You didn't do the seeding part," Tye said once, quietly, not accusing, more like checking a door was locked. Lucas said the tempering was basically done by the fridge anyway. Tye looked at the shelf again, at his own mould sitting there dull and matte while it set, and said nothing more, which Lucas took for agreement. It was not agreement. Tye had spent the whole period on that chocolate, dragging it across the marble, testing a smear on wax paper until it dried in three minutes with a satin finish, and now he was watching Lucas's shortcut sit on the same shelf with his name on it, waiting.

At Tye's station, twenty minutes later, the problem arrived from the other direction. Quentin came over to see the results, and it was Quentin's mould, not Lucas's, that failed first. Quentin tipped his plastic mould over the counter and shook it, and the shells stayed put, four of them, wedged like coins in a drain. He shook harder. One shell cracked at the edge and stayed in place anyway, a brown crescent visible through the plastic.

"Mine too," Lucas said, and turned his own mould over. Nothing moved. He shook it, knocked it on the counter, pried at a shell with the tip of the palette knife and broke off a corner. The pieces came out dull, streaked grey at the shoulder where they had clung to the cavity, no shine anywhere. He looked down the row of failures and felt briefly exonerated, because if everyone's had stuck, the fault was not his shortcut.

Then Tye turned his mould over and the shells dropped out onto the cloth, whole, one after another, with a small sound like buttons on a table. Tye picked one up and snapped it in half. The break was clean and it sounded dry, and the two faces of the piece shone.

Quentin leaned in. "Why do yours come out?" he asked.

"Tempered chocolate shrinks a little while it sets," Tye said. "So it pulls away from the mould."

Lucas turned back to his own tray, where the chocolate was clinging hard to the plastic, and understood that the shine on Tye's shells was the same fact stated twice, once in the surface and once in the clean release. He had thought of tempering as decoration, a finish, the morphology of the thing rather than its structure. The chocolate had not been liquid and then hard, the way he had assumed; it had been ductile all through the cooling, moving and rearranging while it looked inert, and every minute of Tye's stirring had been that rearrangement happening. He could not say whether the fault was in skipping the cooling step or the reheating one, or both; the handout's temperatures were on his wrist and he had ignored all three equally.

There was no time to start over. The bell was in six minutes. Lucas scraped the broken shells into the bin and turned the empty mould upside down, and a last crescent of chocolate dropped out of its cavity, dull, edges ragged. He picked it up and put it in his mouth anyway, and it melted slowly and without any snap at all.

"Tomorrow," Tye said, wiping down the marble slab, "do the stirring part."

"Show me the wrist test," Lucas said, and held out his arm, the temperatures still legible under the chocolate smudge.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine.
story:
The trail behind the school cut through a strip of birch and sumac that the town called a preserve, though James suspected the word flattered it. He had his notebook open against his knee, and Maina walked a slow circle around the bench where he sat, the way she did when she was deciding whether to be patient with him.

"Again," she said. "The mRNA is AUGCCUGGUAAU. Decode it."

James ran his pencil under the letters. He had the codon table copied out from the textbook, three columns of it, and he had gotten fast at looking things up, which he had begun to suspect was not the same as understanding anything. He started at the first letter and counted off three: UGC. Cys. CUG. Leu. GUA. Val. "Cysteine, leucine, valine," he said, and then the rest fell apart into stops and singles, fragments that meant nothing, and he knew it before he finished saying it.

"That's not a protein," Maina said. "That's alphabet soup."

"I did what you told me. Three letters at a time."

"You did it in the wrong place." She sat down on the armrest of the bench and pulled the notebook toward her, tapping the page somewhere above where he had started, though she didn't show him exactly where. He remembered her saying it once, days ago, while he was half listening: translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine. He had filed it away the way he filed most things Ms. Mansour said in that class, as decoration rather than instruction, and now he sat with the letters in front of him and understood that he had been predicated on a false assumption from the very first triplet, that everything downstream had inherited his error.

He counted again. The first A, the U, the G. AUG. Methionine. Then CCU, proline. GGU, glycine. AAU, asparagine. "Met-Pro-Gly-Asn," he said. "That's a real sequence. That could be a real protein."

"That's the answer," Maina said. "For the puzzle, anyway. Ms. Mansour makes them all start with that codon on purpose, so if you don't get methionine first, you know right away you drifted." A jogger passed them on the trail, and a dog off its leash followed at a distance, and James sat looking at the four words in his notebook as if they had arrived from somewhere rather than being assembled by him out of a table.

He had signed up for the science fair late, mostly because his mother had asked why he never signed up for anything, and he had spent two weekends feeling like a dilettante, someone playing at molecular biology with a library book and a set of colored pencils. But something had shifted on the bench, and he tried to say it out loud, because saying things to Maina was how he found out whether they were true. "I keep thinking there are two versions of me doing this," he said. "One that memorizes, and one that actually reads the code. The memorizer got the question wrong and the reader got it right, and I don't know which one shows up at the fair."

Maina considered this with the seriousness she gave to things she intended to argue with. "Maybe they're not opposites. You couldn't have found the start codon if you hadn't memorized the table. You couldn't have noticed the nonsense without knowing what sense looks like." She stood and stretched, then pointed down the trail to where the preserve opened onto a scrubby field, an old fence line standing there, vestigial, marking a boundary between properties that no longer existed as separate farms. "Walk with me. You can tell me the difference between transcription and translation while we go, and I'll correct you."

"Transcription first," James said, falling into step beside her. "DNA to mRNA. Then translation, mRNA to protein, and the AUG is where it starts, methionine first, every time, at least usually." He heard himself say it and found that it held, that the fact sat in his mouth like something he owned instead of something he was borrowing. They passed the fence and the field opened up, warm and full of insect noise, and somewhere ahead the trail split, one branch going back toward the school parking lot and the other toward the creek where nobody officially went.

"Say the whole thing again from the top," Maina said. "Slower this time."

James took a breath and started walking toward the creek.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data.
story:
Sarah counted her kicks off every wall, the way Ms. Aquino had taught the whole team in September, because counting kept her mind from doing the other thing, which was deciding she was cold, or slow, or finished before the set was finished. The pool at six in the morning held a green kind of light that she liked, the lamps still fighting the dark windows. She had made regionals in the hundred free last year as an accident, she felt, and this season she wanted to make it on purpose, which was a different and heavier thing to carry through the water.

At the second turn she heard the argument before she saw it, Reece's voice carrying flat across the shallow end. Reece swam backstroke and read books about baseball for fun, and today he was standing at the clipboard with the coach, arms folded, saying something about Gilovich.

"Nobody believes in the hot hand," the coach said. "Not in my pool. You make the shot or you miss it, and you take the next one the same either way."

"That's not what the data says," Reece said. "In 2018, two economists, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo, showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias. They found evidence of streak shooting in the same data. The exact same data. The paper that killed it."

The coach looked at Reece the way he looked at a false start, and moved practice on.

Sarah had grown up on the other side of that argument without knowing it had sides. Her father watched basketball with the sound off and said hot when a shooter got hot, and she had absorbed it like the smell of chlorine, without question. Then in seventh grade a teacher had said the hot hand was a trick the mind played, that people saw patterns in coin flips, and she had absorbed that too, also without question, which struck her now, hanging on the lane rope, as a strange way to go through a mind. Two beliefs, both smooth, both borrowed, and they had never once been made to touch each other.

She found Reece in the corridor after practice, his hair drying in wrong directions. "Explain it to me like I'm asleep," she said.

"In 1985 Gilovich and his co-authors looked at shooting data from the Celtics and said, okay, after a player makes shots, does he make the next one more often? They didn't find it, so they said the hot hand's a myth. Miller and Sanjurjo showed that analysis had a statistical bias. Then they found evidence of streak shooting in the same data."

"In the same data," Sarah repeated. The same numbers, read once as proof of nothing and then again as proof of something. "So which is true?"

"That's the wrong question," Reece said, and then, being Reece, he laughed at himself for saying it. "It's the right question, actually. It's just hard."

She wanted it to be simple. That was the honest pull of it. She wanted to stand at the blocks believing either that streaks were magic or that they were nothing, because both of those were load-bearing beliefs, things you could push off the wall with. What she had instead was a bias in a 1985 analysis corrected in 2018, and a body of evidence that said streaks were real but real the way weather was real, not the way fate was real.

She tried it out in the water all the following week, and mostly it failed, because a mind in the middle of a hundred free cannot hold a nuance. On Wednesday she hit the third turn leading her heat and felt the hot feeling come over her, the loosened shoulders, the sense of corridors opening, and she thought, irrelevant, and kept counting kicks. On Friday she hit the turn last and felt the cold feeling, the one that said the race was already gone, and she thought, also irrelevant, keep counting, and came back on the final twenty-five to out-touch Ellen by a fingertip.

"See," Ellen said at the gutter, gasping and delighted. "You got hot at the end."

"Maybe," Sarah said. "Or maybe I just didn't get cold."

Ellen frowned at her. "What's the difference?"

Sarah lay back in the water and let it hold her ears so the ceiling sounded far away. She was thinking of the words desensitize, how you could become numb to a thing by hearing it too often, and how she never wanted that to happen to this, to the strange double feeling of holding a fact and a mystery in the same hand. A girl on the team had once said stats were the detractor of sport, that numbers pulled beauty apart like a mechanic pulling an engine, and their coach had shrugged and said the numbers don't care about your feelings either way, and Sarah thought both of those adults had been wrong in the same direction, certain.

She raised her head. "The difference is I don't know yet," she said. "Ask me at regionals."

Ellen pushed off the wall and dove under her, and Sarah watched the bubbles rise and break, one and then two and then a whole streak of them, and she laughed, alone, at what might have been nothing.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and old carpet, and Mr. Chanthavong had cleared a corner of it for her: a folding chair, a lamp with a cracked shade, an amp he said she could use as long as she didn't monetize his kindness by charging her friends to listen. Maria had laughed at that, though she didn't fully understand it until later, when she realized he meant it as a joke about her plan to play at Naima's cousin's birthday party for twenty dollars.

The guitar had come from a yard sale, five dollars, no case. Its provenance was a mystery; the woman selling it said only that it had belonged to her brother, who had moved to Calgary. The strings were dark with use and the sixth string buzzed whenever Maria fretted it, a flat metallic rattle that made her wince. Dave said the strings were dead and she should buy new ones. Maria said new strings cost money, and the twenty dollars from the party was theoretical until she could actually play something.

She had been at it for six weeks. Her fingertips had gone from sore to calloused, and she could switch between three chords without stopping, which was not the same as playing. The problem was the tuner. Dave had installed an app on her phone, and it worked fine for the low strings, but when she tried to tune the highest string, the numbers on the screen made no sense to her. It read 440 for the fifth string, and when she played the note she believed was the same A, only higher, the app read 880. She assumed the app was broken, or the guitar was, or she was.

She texted Naima about it on Thursday night, lying on her bed with the phone held above her face. "Is my tuner broken? It says 440 on one string and 880 on another and I'm playing the same letter, A, both times." Naima replied a few minutes later, in her way, with a screenshot from a music forum and a single line: "A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz." Maria stared at the message, then read it again. She got up, went to the garage in her socks, and played the low A. Four hundred and forty. Then the A at the fifth fret of the first string. Eight hundred and eighty. Exactly double, both times, stable on the screen like two numbers agreeing with each other.

Something about it steadied her. The buzzing sixth string still buzzed, her chords still frayed at the transitions, but the doubled number felt like a door left open a crack. There was a system underneath the thing she was failing at, a system so exact that the same letter in a higher place vibrated at precisely twice the speed of its lower twin. She sat in the garage with the lamp on and worked it out loud, mostly to the amp, which was switched off. If the octaves were doubles, then the frets between them were dividing that doubled distance in a way she couldn't yet name, and she wanted to name it. She wanted it more than she wanted the twenty dollars.

On Saturday Dave came over with a set of strings he'd bought with his birthday money, phosphor bronze, and while he watched she restrung the sixth string herself, following a video, winding the tuning peg until the new string pulled taut and bright. "They say these ones sound warmer," Dave said. "More ductile, or something. They bend easier." Maria tested it, bending the string up at the twelfth fret and hearing the note slide sweetly out of true and back. The buzz was gone.

Mr. Chanthavong appeared at the garage door with two glasses of lemonade and stayed to listen, leaning against the workbench with his arms folded. Maria played the song she'd built for the party, four chords, then a melody line on top, and when she reached the A she played it low and then high, one after the other, listening for the doubling she could now hear as a kind of sameness, a note and its brighter twin. She missed the last chord change. She went back and played it again and missed it differently.

"I don't know if I'm ready for the party," she said, when she'd finished. "It's in two weeks."

Mr. Chanthavong set his glass down on the workbench. "The girl who was here six weeks ago couldn't tune a string."

"But I don't know if it's good. I don't even know what good is yet."

"That's an honest position," he said. "Most people pretend they know."

Maria looked down at the tuner app, still open on her phone, the needle resting at zero. She played the low A, then the high one, watching 440 become 880, and reached for the chord change again.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
story:
Taylor had counted the days until the chemistry showcase at the science museum since Mr. Mansour announced that the student who impressed the visiting panel would be offered the summer internship in the education wing, and she had prepared the way she prepared for everything, with index cards colour-coded by unit, equilibrium written in green because it was her weakest and she knew it.

The exhibit hall smelled of floor wax and dry ice. Dominick walked beside her with his hands in his pockets, and she knew what he wanted before he said it, because he had said it twice on the bus: he wanted the internship too, but for the badge, the laminated badge that said STAFF, which he seemed to believe could emancipate him from being the kid who got picked last in gym. Ashlee trailed behind them eating pretzel pieces from a paper sleeve, wanting, as far as Taylor could tell, only to get through the afternoon without being asked to calculate anything.

The equilibrium display was a long glass case split into two chambers connected by a pump, blue liquid that went pink when the docent, a retired engineer with reading glasses on a chain, added a drop of acid. "The system shifts to oppose the change," she said. "Le Chatelier's principle." She let the colour bloom and settle, bloom and settle, and Taylor watched it the way you watch a tide, something that looked like stillness but never was.

The docent held up a card with a reaction printed on it, nitrogen and hydrogen going to ammonia, and asked why a factory might choose a temperature that gave it less product at the end. Ashlee leaned toward the pretzel stand. Dominick squared his shoulders and said, "They wouldn't. That would be pernicious to the yield, wouldn't it, you'd just lose money," and the docent smiled without correcting him, which Taylor had learned from Mr. Mansour was the worst kind of silence, the kind that meant you were confidently wrong.

Taylor stood at the case and thought about the two directions at once, the way she had taught herself to do during the unit she'd nearly failed. Cold would push the reaction toward ammonia, that was the shift, the system answering the change with opposition. But a system could oppose you all it wanted and still take forever doing it. She said, slowly, testing each word as it left her, "It's exothermic. So low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium." The docent nodded once. "But the plants run hotter," Taylor went on, "because when it's cold the reaction is too slow." The words felt like two planks she was nailing together, and the nail going in was the sound of the pump cycling behind the glass.

"So it's a compromise," Dominick said, and Taylor heard something deflate in him, his answer replaced by hers, his badge drifting a little further out of reach. She looked at him and felt the unfairness of it, that she could want this thing and also want him not to have it, that both wants could sit in her at the same time like the two chambers of the case, connected, shifting.

The docent wrote something on a clipboard and asked Taylor what she would still want to know. That was the question Mr. Mansour always asked, and Taylor had learned that saying "nothing" was the fast way to lose him. "I don't know where the line is," she said. "Between too slow and too little. Who decides what the right temperature is, and whether it's the same answer in a week, or a decade." The docent's glasses swung on their chain as she laughed, short and approving, and made another mark.

Ashlee appeared at Taylor's elbow, brushing salt from her fingers, and said the pretzels were gone and the vending machine on the second floor had the iced tea with the lemon on the can, if anyone cared. The panel was still three exhibits away, and Taylor's index cards stayed in her bag, unneeded and slightly bent. She thought of the weekend, all those hours of green ink, and how they had bought her something she couldn't have predicted, which was the small, unsettling pleasure of not knowing and saying so out loud. Dominick was already walking toward the second floor, calling back that the machine also took his card, and Taylor followed the sound of his voice past the pendulum, its sand tracing its slow, patient arcs.

Ashlee pressed the button for the iced tea, and the can dropped with a thunk.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
story:
The quiz was Thursday, and Ashley had promised Ms. Eze she would come in at lunch to show she understood optimization. That promise had seemed easy to make on Monday. Now it was Wednesday evening, and she sat in the emptying classroom after last bell, drawing parabolas on the whiteboard while Erin leaned against a desk, unwrapping a granola bar.

"Okay," Ashley said. "Revenue is this polynomial. I take the derivative, I set it equal to zero, I solve. Wherever the derivative is zero, that's my maximum. Done. Can we go?"

"That's what Graham said too," Erin said, chewing. "He got it wrong on the practice sheet. Ms. Eze circled his answer and wrote one word. 'Graph?'"

"Graham says a lot of things. Half of what he says is specious. Yesterday he told me you could park in the lot behind the gym because the no-parking ordinance only applies during school hours, and I got a ticket."

"You got the ticket because you parked across two spaces."

"Focus. The derivative is the slope. If the slope is zero, the graph is flat for a second. Flat means the top of a hill. That's the whole point of this unit. Why else would she teach it?"

Erin shrugged and copied the polynomial off Ashley's notebook, a cubic thing Ms. Eze had requisitioned from some old exam, real numbers about the price of printing yearbooks and the number sold. "Then do it on this one. I'll watch."

Ashley worked it out on the board. The derivative came out clean, three x squared, zero at exactly x equals zero. "See," she said, tapping the point. "Maximum. At zero. I'll tell Ms. Eze tomorrow that I solved it in four minutes."

Erin was quiet in a way that made Ashley suspicious. "What."

"Graph it."

"I don't need to graph it. The algebra is right."

"Then graphing it will take you thirty seconds and prove you're right." Erin held out a marker. "Unless you'd rather find out tomorrow, in front of her, during lunch, with the quiz on Thursday."

Ashley took the marker. She plotted the cubic point by point, first some negative values, then through zero, then the positives, and stood back, and felt something shift in her stomach. The curve came up from the bottom left, flattened for the smallest moment at the origin, and then kept right on rising. There was no hill. There was no valley. It was more like a road leveling out briefly before climbing again, and her "maximum" sat in the middle of the climb, nowhere near the top of anything.

"That's not a maximum," she said slowly. "The slope is zero there, and it's not a maximum."

"Which is what Ms. Eze wanted Graham to see, I think." Erin came closer to the board. "So what is it, then? Just a flat spot?"

"I don't know what it is." Ashley said it out loud and heard how it sounded, and did not take it back. "I know what it isn't. The rule I had, zero derivative means maximum, that was never the rule. It was a shortcut that worked on the parabolas because they happened to have hills." She drew both graphs side by side, the parabola with its true peak, the cubic sailing through its pause. "So the derivative finds the flat places. Then you have to look at the graph to see what kind of flat place it is. The algebra finds the candidates and the picture tells you who won."

"Who won."

"Or nobody won. In this one nobody won. The function just keeps going up." She looked at the clock above the door and realized she had twenty minutes before the building locked. "Tomorrow, when she asks, I'm going to say it like that. Derivative first, graph second, and if it's a flat spot in the middle of a climb, you say so instead of pretending it's a peak."

"You're going to admit you don't know what the flat spot is called?"

"I'll admit it. She can tell me the name after. If I pretend I already know everything, I'll do what Graham did, and Graham is currently eating lunch alone with his circled answer." Ashley capped the marker, then uncapped it once more and, under the cubic, wrote in small letters: keeps rising through this point. She stepped back and looked at the two curves, one honest hill and one long climb with a catch in it.

"Okay," she said, and picked up her bag. "Same time tomorrow. Bring your own markers."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
The bus smelled of diesel and cold vinyl, and Abigail had the whole back seat to herself except for the folder on her knees. Inside the folder was the rubric from last week's semifinal, where the judges had circled the same phrase twice: presentation rushed, visuals late. The visuals were Kason's slides. He was sitting four rows up with his headphones on, bobbing his head in small, happy increments, and at three o'clock they would present again, which gave her two hours and forty minutes to say something she had been swallowing since Friday.

She had tried on Saturday, in the group chat, and it had gone badly in the way that text always goes badly. She had typed "the slides came in at midnight, we had no time," which was true, and Kason had replied with a thumbs-up, which was somehow worse than an argument. Rayyan had messaged her privately afterward: say it out loud, not in writing. She had thought about that for two days.

In the folder, under the rubric, was a photocopied page from her psychology unit, the one Mr. Huang had assigned back in October and she had read on a whim last night at eleven, looking for anything. Certain sentence shapes, the page said, had been promoted by the psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming. Abigail read the examples twice. "I felt stuck when the slides came in late." It was almost eerie, like the page had been in her folder for months, waiting.

She tried it out under her breath, watching the guardrail stutter past the window. "I felt stuck." It sounded thin. "You ruined the semifinal," she thought, and that sounded strong but wrong, like a door slammed on a room she still needed to walk into. Somewhere between the two was the sentence she actually wanted, and she could not find it by feel alone. She pulled the folder closer and wrote, in the margin of the rubric, both versions, then crossed out the second one, then wrote it again. Congenital honesty, her grandmother called it, the kind you were born with and never learned to aim.

Two rows up, Rayyan was watching the back of Abigail's head in the window's reflection, the way her pen moved and stopped, moved and stopped. He knew about the chat. Everyone knew about the chat; Kason had shown him the thumbs-up with a laugh, as if it were nothing, and Rayyan had laughed too, because the truth was he had also wanted to throttle Kason at midnight on Thursday, refreshing the shared drive while the practice room got hotter and hotter. But he had said nothing, and Abigail had said nothing in any real way, and now the three of them were on a bus heading toward a podium they had no chance of reaching if somebody did not speak. He wondered whether it would be him. He hoped, cowardly and sincerely, that it would be her.

Kason turned around eventually, because he always turned around; it was congenital with him, this inability to sit facing forward. "You're studying?" he said. "On the bus?"

"Practicing," Abigail said.

"For what?"

She looked at him. His headphones were around his neck, and he was grinning, and she thought, with a clarity that surprised her, that she had no idea whether he even knew the slides had been late, or whether he knew and had decided not to know. That was the part she could not resolve from the window, and she was tired of resolving things from windows. "Can you sit here a second?"

He dropped into the seat across the aisle, still grinning, though the grin downshifted into something more careful. Rayyan, two rows up, turned slightly sideways in his own seat, pretending to sleep.

"Last week," Abigail said, and then stopped, because "last week you" was the top of a cliff. She looked down at the margin where she had written both sentences. "I felt stuck when the slides came in late," she said. "We'd been practicing all night and I couldn't run my part against anything real. I felt like the whole thing was an amalgam of two different talks, mine and something I'd never seen."

Kason's grin was gone now. "They were late," he said. "I know they were late."

"I'm not saying it to make you feel bad."

"Then why are you saying it in that weird order?"

Rayyan spoke from his seat without opening his eyes. "Gordon called them I-messages," he said. "Sixties guy. We read the same page."

"Fine, don't explain my own folder to me," Abigail said, and Kason laughed, a real one this time, and the sound transmuted something in the aisle between them, though she could not have said what, or into what.

"I kept rebuilding the deck," Kason said. "I thought it would be better and it was just later. That's on me." He was quiet for a stop sign, for the hiss of the doors. "For today, they're done. They've been done since Sunday. I just didn't want to show anyone in case they were bad again."

"So we have forty hours of slides and no practice against them," Abigail said, but she said it lightly, and she was already pulling her laptop out of her bag. "Two hours. Show me now."

He leaned across the aisle, and the screen lit between them, and outside the guardrail gave way to the long grey approach to the campus.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
The girl's name was Dani, and she had suggested the mall because it was the only place she could think of where two people could walk around without anyone expecting them to buy anything. Adam had agreed on the theory that a first date with built-in exits was a merciful design. He'd ironed a shirt for it, which his mother had noticed and mercifully not commented on.

They met by the fountain at three. Dani was already there, spinning a quarter on the tile, and she said he was late by four minutes, which was true, and that she'd forgive him if he bought her a pretzel, which seemed fair. They walked the long loop past the shoe stores and the phone kiosks, and she talked mostly about her old school, the one she'd transferred out of in November, in a way that was funny on the surface and had something underneath it that Adam couldn't read yet and didn't push at.

At the arcade she beat him twice at air hockey, and when he laughed at his own loss she grabbed his forearm to emphasize a point about his defense, and it hurt more than he let on. He registered the marks of four fingers and thought, generously, that she was just physical, that some people narrated with their hands. She did it again by the claw machines, harder, when he joked that she was acting like a despot with the joystick. "I am a despot," she said, pleased, and squeezed, and he laughed, though the laugh came out thinner than he intended.

Ryley was working the customer service desk that afternoon, and Adam had known that, and had half-hoped they'd pass without notice. No such luck. Ryley clocked them from across the atrium the way he clocked everything, with the patience of someone whose job was mostly returning lost mittens. On their third lap, when Dani had gone into a store to try on sunglasses, Ryley came over and leaned against the planter.

"Your arm's red," Ryley said. Not a question.

"She's enthusiastic."

"She grabbed you twice by the fountain and once at the arcade. I could see it from the desk." Ryley picked at the planter's mulch. His whole manner said he'd rehearsed this in his head and was now abandoning the script. "Senior year, we had this unit in health. The CDC did this survey in 2021, the Youth Risk Behavior Survey, and about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence. One in twelve. And that was the ones who said so."

"I'm not in high school anymore," Adam said, which sounded, even to him, like a bad argument.

"Neither were half of them when it started." Ryley shrugged, embarrassed by his own earnestness, which he usually treated as something to be ironized away. "I'm not saying she's a supervillain. I'm saying I watched it three times in forty minutes and my neck got tight. Do whatever you want." He wanted, Adam understood, to be released from having noticed. He wanted Adam to laugh it off so the noticing could be filed as nothing, and he also wanted Adam not to laugh it off, and he was stuck between the two like a man with an arm in each door.

Dani came out of the store wearing enormous sunglasses, capricious in her moods, radiant and then sharp and then radiant again, and asked who the friend was. Ryley introduced himself with a formality that was its own small speech, and Dani said, "He was just leaving," pleasantly, and Ryley looked at Adam for one second, waiting to see which of them Adam would obey.

Adam walked Ryley as far as the pretzel stand. Two ways of thinking sat in him, arguing politely. One said she touched him the way weather touches a coastline, without malice, without much thought at all, and a person deserved more than one afternoon before being filed under a statistic. The other said the body keeps its own records, that his arm had ached for ten minutes after the fountain and he had smiled through it, and that smiling through it was exactly the reflex he should be suspicious of. He could not make them agree. What he could do was stop pretending the ache wasn't information.

"Tell her," he said to Ryley at the counter. "About the arm. Not the survey, just the arm. If she grabs it again, tell her you saw it."

"She'll hate me."

"Probably." Adam paid for the pretzel. "Do it anyway."

He carried the pretzel back through the atrium, past the fountain, and found Dani waiting by the quarter-spinning tile with her sunglasses pushed up into her hair. She looked at him for a long moment, the way she'd looked at the air hockey table before her first goal.

"You told your friend to watch me," she said.

Adam handed her the pretzel, held the door of the arcade open, and said, "Best two out of three."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
The grocery store sat on the alluvial flat where the river slowed and dropped its silt, and behind the loading dock the land narrowed to a weedy isthmus between the water and the drainage pond, a place Tyler had crossed a hundred times without ever thinking about soil. Today he crossed the parking lot in his one collared shirt, carrying a folder with his birth certificate and a pen that didn't work, because Ms. Lin had told him to bring both, and because he wanted this job more than he had wanted anything he could name.

She met him at the service desk and walked him through the paperwork at a pace that suggested she had done this four hundred times and would do it four hundred more. "Sign here, here, initials there," she said, and when he asked about the box marked with letters he didn't understand, she tapped it once. "You'll see it on your first check," she said, and moved on to the emergency contact line, where he wrote his mother's number and, after a pause, his own beneath it.

Two weeks later he stood at the time clock with Loik, holding an envelope he had already opened in the parking lot. He had done the math in his head all the way home and then again on paper, and the numbers refused to agree. Sixty-two hours at eleven dollars an hour should have been six hundred eighty-two dollars. The check said six hundred thirty-nine and change, and the stub had a column of small print that subtracted things he hadn't agreed to.

"Mine's short too," Loik said, tearing his own envelope open with his teeth. "Every check. I asked my cousin and he said welcome to being a worker, which is not an answer."

Tyler spread the stub on the hood of Loik's car and read it line by line, the way he read proofs in geometry, assuming nothing was true until the columns balanced. There was a federal line, small, and a state line, smaller, and then a line that took more than both of them. It had taken six point two percent of his wages exactly, which he verified twice with the division, and the label beside it said Social Security. "That's the biggest one," he said. "It's 6.2 percent. I did the math."

Anissa came out with her own check folded into her back pocket and leaned over the stub, squinting at it. She worked front end, register three, and she had opinions about everything the back of the store did. "That one never stops," she said. "Well, almost never. Ms. Lin says it goes up to a wage limit, some amount per year, and then it stops for the year, but nobody here makes that much, so it just comes out." She shrugged. "It's for when you're old, supposedly."

Inside, Ms. Lin was stacking returned goods onto a cart, and Tyler went to her with the stub still in his hand. He didn't complain; he asked whether the percentage was right, whether it was supposed to be that much, whether there was a form he'd signed wrong. She looked at the stub, then at him, and something in her face shifted from supervisor to something older. "It's right," she said. "I've paid it since 1989." She handed the stub back and went on stacking cans of pears.

He walked home along the river path, and he found he could hold two things at once without either one breaking. The money was his, in the sense that he had stood in the dairy cooler for sixty-two hours stacking yogurt, and it was not his, in the sense that some of it had never been available to him at all, had been spoken for before he was hired. He had always been able to compartmentalize, to put school in one drawer and home in another, but this didn't fit in a drawer. It was more like the isthmus behind the store, a narrow connection between two bodies of water you'd otherwise call separate, and he could stand on it and be touched by both. What he couldn't decide, walking, was whether the arrangement was fair or merely old, and whether those were even different questions, and he noticed that not deciding felt less like weakness than like honesty.

On Monday he asked Ms. Lin for more hours anyway. She looked up from the schedule pinned behind the service desk, pencil in hand, and considered him for a long moment over her glasses. "Saturdays too?" she said.

"Saturdays too," Tyler said, and she wrote his name into the empty boxes.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
Logan had chosen mayonnaise from scratch the way other people chose tattoos: with total confidence and no research. Dinner was supposed to be his gift to his parents for their anniversary, breaded chicken and a bowl of homemade aioli that Suri had sworn was "basically just oil and an egg," which was, he would later reflect, a little like saying a bridge was basically just rocks.

He set the bowl on the counter between the toaster and his phone, where Suri's texts glowed up at him. one yolk, whisk, add oil slow, she'd written. VERY slow. Theodore, cc'd into the group chat against his will, had replied only: mayonnaise is a contrivance invented to punish teenagers. Logan had ascribed this to jealousy, since Theodore once set fire to instant noodles.

The first yolk went in glossy and orange, and Logan began adding oil drop by drop, whisking with the wrist motion he'd seen in a video at two in the morning. For a glorious minute it worked. The mixture thickened, turned pale gold, clung to the whisk. He felt like a chemist, or a wizard, or at minimum a person who could feed his family. Then his attention drifted to the chicken in the pan, his wrist sped up to match the music, the oil went in a glug instead of a drop, and the whole thing curdled into something repellent: a lake of oil with a sad, watery island floating in the middle of it.

He stared at it. He poked it with the whisk. He took a photograph and sent it to the group chat with no caption, and Suri's reply came back in seconds: it broke. Theodore's came back a second after that: it died. u murdered it.

His grandmother, who had been sitting at the kitchen table doing the crossword and pretending not to supervise, slid her chair back and came over in her slippers. She looked into the bowl the way one looks at a badly parked car. "Too fast," she said, which Logan felt was truculent under the circumstances, given that she had witnessed the entire catastrophe and said nothing until now.

"I'll start over," he said.

"Get another yolk," she said, and separated one into a clean bowl with a crack of the shell so crisp it sounded like punctuation. "Whisk it. Then the broken one, spoonful by spoonful." She did not explain why. She tapped the counter twice, as if the counter itself were an accomplice, and went back to seven across.

Logan whisked the fresh yolk until it loosened, then added the curdled mixture a spoonful at a time, feeling extremely stupid and slightly hopeful. Somewhere around the fourth spoonful, the yolk grabbed the oil. The whole thing pulled together under his whisk, thickened, turned that pale gold again, became mayonnaise. He stopped and looked at it. The oil that had been a separate, greasy lake was gone, suspended somehow in the liquid, held there by something in the yolk. He pulled out his phone, because if you can't Google at a moment like that, when can you, and read with his mouth slightly open. "Lecithin and proteins," he said out loud. "From the yolk. They're emulsifiers, they hold the oil droplets in the water." He looked up at his grandmother. "That's what just happened? That's why yours never breaks?"

"It's why patience never breaks," his grandmother said, which was not an answer, and Logan suspected she knew the word lecithin perfectly well and was withholding it out of principle. Or maybe she'd never known it, only the spoonful-by-spoonful of it, which was a kind of knowledge too, the kind that lives in wrists. He couldn't decide which he'd rather ascribe to her: secret science or fifty years of rescue operations. Both were probably true, and both were probably incomplete, which was, he was beginning to notice, how most true things arrived.

The chicken came off the pan golden, and he'd even remembered to flip it before the smoke alarm remembered him. He spooned the mayonnaise, his mayonnaise, resurrected, into his mother's good bowl and set it beside the lemon wedges. Suri texted a crown emoji. Theodore texted a slow clap. His parents came through the door at six, and his mother said, "You cooked?" in the voice of someone who has found a dog doing taxes.

At dinner his father dipped a piece of chicken, held it up, and said, "Logan. This is real mayonnaise." Logan opened his mouth to explain lecithin, the emulsifiers, the spoonful-by-spoonful rescue, and then closed it again and just shrugged, while across the table his grandmother raised one eyebrow at him over her glass of water and went back to her crossword.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
The ballot box on the folding table was actually a shoebox wrapped in leftover birthday paper, and I want it on record that I, Savannah, aged sixteen and a half, which for voting purposes in my own head is basically eighteen, had nothing to do with choosing the paper. Rainbows. For a student council election. Kiersten had wrapped it, and Kiersten had also hand-lettered the sign above it, POLLING PLACE, COMMUNITY HALL, because our school gym flooded on Tuesday and Mr. Pérez had swooped in with a key and a thermos and said, "Democracy does not wait for mops."

He was wrong about that, historically speaking, but nobody argued with Mr. Pérez before nine in the morning.

Here is the problem. Our year had voted to make voting in the student election compulsory. Not the teachers, not the administration, us, in a fit of civic enthusiasm three weeks ago when everyone was still high on the mock parliament unit. Fine people five dollars if they don't vote without a valid reason. The hall emptied at six o'clock sharp, when Mr. Pérez locked the doors for a pottery class, and it was already five forty, and I still hadn't decided between Cassius and Kiersten, who were both standing by the juice table pretending not to watch me.

"I'm not undemocratic," I'd told Cassius on Monday, while he was stapling posters. "I'm just saying, making people vote is like making people dance at a wedding. Some of us have reasons." That was before I understood what I now understood, which is that I was going to vote anyway. I always was. The rule wasn't for me. The rule was for the forty-one students who would otherwise be at home, and I had been dressing up my laziness as a principle, which is a thing I do, apparently, and would like to stop doing before college.

"You know where the fine idea came from, right?" Cassius said now, drifting over with two cups of juice, handing me one like a bribe, though I had already decided not to be bribed by juice. "Australia. Compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925. If you don't vote and you don't have a valid reason, you can be fined. Real money. Adults."

"Since 1925," Kiersten repeated, arriving on my other side, which is what Kiersten does, arrives. "A hundred years of people trudging to the polls or paying up. I find it beautiful. You find it bossy. We've had this fight."

"It is a little bossy," I said. "But it's also the only system where the sitting-around-on-the-couch people get counted. Otherwise the whole election is decided by whoever's most excited, and the most excited people are usually the angriest people, and the angriest people are usually the ones who want a chocolate fountain installed in the cafeteria." I looked at Cassius. His entire platform was a chocolate fountain. He had called it, in his speech, "a small, munificent gesture," which he'd clearly looked up, and which had made even the teachers laugh.

"It's not just hedonism," Cassius said, wounded. "It's morale. It's school spirit, in liquid form."

"It's hedonism in liquid form," Kiersten said.

"Both of you," I said, "are making this very hard." And it was true that Cassius's platform was one expensive joke, and Kiersten's platform was a twelve-point plan that used the phrase "long-term budgeting" unironically, and the truth I had been circling all week was that the points didn't cancel out. I wanted the boring competent one to run things and the silly one to keep everyone showing up. The compulsory rule did the showing-up part. Maybe the chocolate fountain could underwrite the rest. That's not a metaphor; Cassius had actually gotten the hardware store to underwrite half the cost, which should have disqualified him and instead made me like him more.

Five fifty-two. Behind me, Mr. Pérez had begun stacking chairs with the slow menace of a man whose pottery class started at six thirty.

"You can spoil your ballot," Kiersten offered. "Draw a cat on it. People do that in countries with compulsory voting, I read. It's a whole tradition."

"I don't want to draw a cat." I took the pencil, which was golf pencil length and somehow the most official object in the building. "I want to vote for the fountain and hope you win anyway."

"You can't do both," Cassius said, delighted, watching me write.

"Watch me," I said, and folded the rainbow paper in half, and dropped it in the shoebox before either of them could see which name I'd actually put the X under.

Mr. Pérez called five fifty-five from the door, already turning the key.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
The festival had closed off two blocks of Rueben Street, and Hunter's mother had claimed a patch of shade near the bookstall before the crowd thickened. Hunter stood beside her with his phone out, scanning the entrance for Mustafa, who had texted "parking, 10 min" eleven minutes ago. The gurdwara's nagar kirtan was meant to arrive at noon, and after that the langar would open, and his grandmother had been clear: everyone sits together, so be back before the food starts.

"Who are you waiting for?" his mother asked, not looking up from a table of prayer books.

"Mustafa. From chem class. He wanted to see it." Hunter had invited him almost by accident, a sentence thrown out during a lab about reflux, and then Mustafa had actually said yes, which turned a casual offer into something Hunter now felt responsible for. He wasn't sure what his job was, exactly. Guide? Translator? He'd grown up inside this and had never once needed words for it.

Mustafa appeared finally at the barricade, wearing the same gray hoodie he wore to every class, looking around with the particular alertness of someone who doesn't want to look like he's looking around. Hunter waved him over. "You're just in time. The procession's about to come through."

"Is that the thing with the float?" Mustafa asked. "Braydon said there'd be a float. He wanted to come too but he had work."

There was a float, though Hunter had never called it that in his life; in the family's vernacular it was just the palki, and he found himself hesitating over which word to hand Mustafa, the inside word or the outside one. He settled on both. "The palki. Palanquin, sort of. The Guru Granth Sahib travels on it." He caught himself before he added more, because he could hear how it would sound, a museum tour, and Mustafa hadn't asked for a museum.

The procession arrived in a slow river of orange and saffron, drummers keeping a rhythm that seemed to delimit the whole street, marking where the crowd began and ended more firmly than any barricade. Bystanders stepped forward to bow as the palki passed, and Mustafa watched them with his hands in his pockets. "Can I do that?" he asked quietly. "Or is it, like, members only?"

Hunter considered the question longer than it probably needed. "Anyone can bow if they want to. Nobody's checking credentials." He said it lightly, but it reminded him of the thing his grandfather always said at langar time, that the food is for everyone, and he wondered, not for the first time, whether Mustafa would find that part strange or whether he'd shrug and eat. He realized he wanted him to shrug and eat, and that the wanting made him nervous, which felt tautological somehow, wanting a thing and dreading the test of it at once.

The palki passed, and the crowd began moving toward the community hall where the langar was being laid out. Hunter's grandmother found them near the door, pressing a paper plate into Mustafa's hands before he could speak. "Beta, sit, sit, they're starting." Inside, rows of mats ran the length of the floor, and volunteers moved down them with buckets of dal and trays of roti, serving everyone the same, wherever they had landed. Mustafa lowered himself cross-legged between Hunter and an elderly man Hunter had never seen before in his life, and Ms. Hussain, his old grade ten English teacher, settled across the row with a nod of recognition.

"So this is free," Mustafa said, low, as the volunteer spooned dal onto his plate. "For anyone? Like, any religion?"

"Anyone," Hunter said. "Doesn't matter who you are. Everyone eats on the floor, same food, same level." He heard his grandmother's voice in his own and didn't mind. "That's kind of the point." He didn't try to say what the point was, because he wasn't sure he could, and because Mustafa was already tearing his roti, watching the volunteer move down the row treating the elderly man, Ms. Hussain, and a squirming kid with identical, unhurried fairness.

They ate. Mustafa went back for seconds and got them without asking anybody's permission, which struck Hunter as the correct response, better than any thank-you speech. When they finally stood to go, brushing crumbs from their jeans, Ms. Hussain caught Hunter's eye. "You'll bring him again?" she said, and Mustafa answered before Hunter could, mouth full of the last of his roti: "He doesn't get a vote."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In his 1961 book What Is History?, E. H. Carr described history as 'an unending dialogue between the present and the past'.
story:
The cursor blinked in the empty document while the rain on the window worked itself down to a diminuendo, and Evan had written nothing but his name. The essay was due at midnight. Mr. Fischer's prompt sat at the top of the assignment page: "Choose a source about the Hartwell memorial and explain what it tells us. Then explain what it leaves out." Evan's grandfather had taken him to that memorial every May since he was six, and had always said the same thing, that the stone soldier honored the boys from this town who never came home from France. That was the version Evan had believed until Tuesday, when Laura had shown him a photocopied page from the town's 1927 newspaper in the school library.

"Look at the date," she had said, tapping the page. The paper was from April, and the article described the dedication as a rally, complete with a speech about standing ready for the next war. The stone soldier had gone up eight years after the armistice, at a moment when the whole country was arguing about whether to build up the army again. "So which one is the memorial about?" Laura had asked. "The dead, or the next war?"

Evan typed a search and scrolled. The first results did not augur well: a genealogy site, a parking notice, someone's Flickr album. Then he found a scanned page from a college course, a reading list, and on it a title that stopped him. What Is History?, by E. H. Carr, published in 1961. He opened the preview and ran his eye down the highlighted line, and read it twice, and read it a third time with his hand flat on the desk.

He picked up his phone. "Jaxson. You around?"

"For another hour. What's wrong?"

"Nothing's wrong. Listen to this." Evan read the line aloud, slowly, feeling his way through it. "Carr called it an unending dialogue between the present and the past."

There was a pause, and the sound of Jaxson's recalcitrant printer grinding through a jam somewhere in the background. "Okay. And?"

"Think about the memorial. Grandpa reads it one way because he grew up on the sacrifice story. The 1927 paper reads it another way because that's what it was printed to do. Nobody's lying. The questions people bring to it are different, so the answers are different." Evan was standing now, pacing the short distance between his desk and his bed, the phone on speaker. "So maybe history isn't the stone. It's the argument about the stone, and the argument doesn't end because the present keeps changing."

"That's either really smart or you're stalling," Jaxson said. "How many words do you have?"

"Nineteen. My name counts twice."

"Write, then. Send it to me after."

Evan sat back down. The document stared at him, and he began typing the boring parts first, the description of the monument, the inscription, the location at the corner of the green where the school buses turn. Facts, he had learned somewhere, were the easy portion. It was the meaning of facts that took the work. He typed a paragraph about the newspaper, a paragraph about his grandfather, and then stopped, because he could hear the two paragraphs contradicting each other and he did not yet know how to hold them both.

He got up and went to the shelf behind his father's desk, where his grandfather's old box of clippings had sat since they cleared out the apartment last spring. Evan had avoided the box. That was the thing he had not told Laura or Jaxson, that his grandfather was nine months gone and Evan had not opened the box once. Now he knelt on the floor and lifted the lid.

On top lay the program from the 1927 dedication. The committee list was printed inside, neat columns of names, and near the bottom of the second column Evan found the name he was bracing for without knowing he was bracing for it: his great-great-grandfather, listed as a member of the monument committee. Beneath the program, folded into a small square, was a typed letter, and when Evan smoothed it open he saw it was addressed to his grandfather, then a boy, from a man whose name matched the chairman of that committee. The letter thanked the boy for singing at the dedication and said the monument would keep the memory of his father's regiment alive, and would remind the town, the letter said, of what readiness costs.

Evan read it twice, the way he had read Carr. So the committee man had wanted both things at once, the mourning and the rallying, grief and the argument for the next war folded into one stone figure with a rifle at parade rest. His grandfather had kept the program and the letter for ninety years' worth of keeping, and had chosen, every May, to hand Evan only one of the two meanings. Maybe that was the present talking to the past, too, Evan thought, a grandfather selecting what a boy was ready to hear.

He went back to the computer and deleted his last paragraph, the one where he had tried to declare a winner between the two readings. In its place he wrote that the memorial did not contain a single meaning to be dug out like a coin, that the 1927 paper and his grandfather and he himself were three voices in a conversation the town had been having with that stone for almost a century, and that his own question, a teenager's question about why we build soldiers instead of planting trees, was simply the newest voice in the room. He kept in the uncertainty: he did not know whether his grandfather had ignored the letter's message or had understood it completely and rejected it, and he wrote that down too, that some of the past stays silent no matter how hard you press it.

At 11:40 he sent the file to Jaxson, then sat for a moment with the box still open on the floor beside him, the program and the letter side by side on the carpet. He took a photograph of both, sent that too, and typed, "This is the part I left out of the essay."

Jaxson replied a minute later. "You should have put it in."

"Maybe next year," Evan typed back, and closed the lid of the box, gently, the way you close a door on someone sleeping.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
story:
Mya got the job on a Tuesday, which felt wrong, because jobs were supposed to start on Mondays, and this one started with a whistle around her neck and a red tube under her arm while the morning sun came off the water like a struck bell. The pool sat on an alluvial flat behind the levee, so close to the river that on quiet days you could hear barge engines pushing through the brown water, and Ms. Farah-Ali, the manager, had spent the whole orientation pointing at things Mya was now responsible for keeping people from drowning near.

"Two weeks' notice," Sameer said that first lunch break, dangling his sandals off the picnic table. "When you quit, you have to give two weeks. That's just how jobs work. It's like a law of the universe."

"It's not a law of the universe."

"It's a law of something. My cousin gave one day's notice at the movie theater and they blacklisted him. He can never see a movie in this county again."

"Blacklisted from movies," Anis said, from somewhere inside his sandwich. "That's the saddest sentence I've ever heard."

Mya wasn't planning to quit. But swim season started in August, and her club coach wanted morning practices, and the lifeguard schedule was already a wall of 6 a.m. shifts, and she liked to know her exits before she committed to a room. That was the whole reason she'd read the employee handbook cover to cover on her break instead of eating, which Anis called "the most Mya thing" he'd ever witnessed. Page eleven, between the sunscreen policy and a paragraph about lightning, she found it: employment was at-will, and either the employer or the worker could end the job at any time, for any reason that was not illegal. She read it three times. The pool could let her go on a Wednesday for no reason at all. And she could walk out the same way. The door swung both directions, and nobody had promised to hold it.

She thought of Coach Reyes, two summers ago, standing at the chain-link fence in the flat gray light before practice. He had cut a girl named Priya from the team between seasons, no meeting, no explanation, just a list posted on the fence with names on it and hers not among them. Priya had cried into her goggles. Mya had been fourteen and had assumed that was simply the way the world worked, that the adults held all the doors. Now she sat at a picnic table with a handbook on her knees revising the whole picture: the doors had handles on both sides. Priya hadn't needed a reason to leave either. She just hadn't known it. Maybe none of them had known it.

"It's called at-will," she told Sameer at closing, while they racked the rescue tubes. "I read it in the handbook. Either side can end it, any time, for any reason that isn't illegal. So no, you don't have to give notice. Not legally."

Sameer stood there with a tube half-hooked on the rack, betrayed by the universe. "But my cousin."

"Your cousin chose to be nice about it. That's different from having to."

"Okay, but." He hung the tube properly. "Would you? Just leave them short a guard on a Saturday?"

And there it was, the part the handbook didn't cover. Legally free wasn't the same as free, exactly. Ms. Farah-Ali had already covered three no-call no-shows herself this month, arriving at 5:45 in her windbreaker with her hair still pinned from wherever her real life was. The rule told Mya what she could do. It said nothing about what she ought. She held both ideas the way she'd once held a flutter kick and a breaststroke pull at the same time, waiting to see if her body, or her conscience, would figure out how to make them one motion.

The whistle thing happened on Thursday. A boy went under near the deep-end rope and came up coughing before Mya was even off her stand; the mother, sunscreen-slick and furious, said the guard had been on her phone. Mya hadn't been. Sameer, rotating past on the deck, said flatly, "She was scanning, I watched her," and the security camera, when Ms. Farah-Ali pulled it up in the office with Mya standing there sweating in her whistle, exonerated her completely: eleven seconds of eyes sweeping the water, phone face-down on the stand. Ms. Farah-Ali printed nothing, filed nothing, just turned the monitor toward the mother and let the footage talk.

"You did it right," Ms. Farah-Ali said afterward, quietly, in the office that smelled of chlorine and old towels. "Which is why I'd hate to lose you in August. But if you need to go, you go. That's the deal we all signed." She said it without ceremony, the way you'd say the pool closes at seven.

Mya found Sameer at the picnic table, rinsing his sunglasses in the drinking fountain like a barbarian. "So I talked to Ms. Farah-Ali," she said. "About August."

"The ideologue has thoughts," Anis announced, arriving with the first aid kit he was supposed to be restocking.

"I'm not an ideologue. I just think people should be decent."

"I agree," Mya said. "I'm going to give notice anyway. Not because I have to. Because I want to be the kind of person the handbook doesn't have to explain."

Sameer put his sunglasses on, drip-drying, and looked at her over the top of them. "So you read a rule, decided to break it, and you're calling that a character."

"I'm calling it a considered position. There's a difference."

"Prove it," Sameer said, and nodded toward the water, where the afternoon lesson kids were piling in at the shallow end like dropped groceries. "Considered position, chair three, whistle ready."

Mya climbed the stand.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: If air resistance is ignored, a projectile's horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight, because no horizontal force acts on it.
story:
The Tuesday quiz came back with a red circle around problem four, and Gabriel had gotten it wrong in a way he could not immediately see. He had split the launch into horizontal and vertical pieces, as Mr. Ba had shown, but somewhere between the drawing and the arithmetic the pieces had stopped talking to each other. He carried the paper to the back of the room where Atticus was copying homework off his phone.

"Horizontal velocity stays the same the whole flight," Atticus said, not looking up. "That's the whole trick. It doesn't slow down at all."

"That can't be right," Gabriel said. "Everything slows down."

"Not sideways. Nothing's pushing on it sideways, so it just keeps going." Atticus tapped the page. "Vertical's the mess. Sideways, it's boring."

Gabriel did not believe him. It sounded like one of those shortcuts that worked on quizzes and fell apart in the real world, and he said so, and Atticus said he was welcome to impugn the physics if he could find something that disagreed. Haley, who sat near the window and had finished the quiz early, turned around and said the argument was pure semantics, that "slowing down" and "changing velocity" were different claims, and that Gabriel was losing on the second one even if he won the first. Gabriel said he would settle it himself.

The skate park behind the rec center had a wooden ledge about a meter and a half high with a long concrete runway before it. On Saturday mornings a cluster of older skaters used it as a launch, rolling off at whatever speed they carried and landing in the flat below. Gabriel arrived with a tape measure, a stopwatch he'd borrowed from the chemistry lab, and a notebook. Haley came because she said she wanted to watch him be wrong in person. Atticus brought his board and no intention of using it.

The first skater they asked refused to be timed. The second agreed, rolled off the ledge, and Haley clicked the stopwatch while Gabriel laid the tape from the base of the ledge to the scuff mark the wheels left. Half a second, give or take her thumb. Two meters and change. Gabriel wrote both numbers down and then crouched at the scuff mark like he was reading a crime scene.

"If he left the ledge going four meters a second sideways," he said, "and he was in the air for half a second, then he lands two meters out. Four times point five."

"Congratulations," Haley said. "That's multiplication."

"But that means the sideways speed at the landing is the same as at the ledge." He said it slowly, testing the sentence before he committed to it. "He doesn't lose any of it on the way down. Half a second of falling and the sideways part just keeps going like the fall isn't happening."

They ran it again with a younger skater, slower off the ledge, and the numbers came out the same shape: less speed, less distance, but the ratio held. Whatever sideways speed each skater left with, they still had all of it when they landed. Gabriel sat on the curb and worked through it in the notebook, dividing and multiplying, crossing out his quiz attempt in the margin. Haley looked over his shoulder and pointed out that he was still assuming the air did nothing. He conceded the point. Wind would drag on it, a little. On the quiz, apparently, you were supposed to leave the air out of it entirely, and under that condition the sideways speed never changed at all, from the first instant to the last.

"What I still don't get," Gabriel said, "is why it's allowed to stay the same. Nothing tells me why."

"That's the one part nobody's offered you," Haley said. "You watched it happen. Whether it's allowed is a different question."

They stayed until the older skaters cleared out and the park went quiet except for the chain links ticking in the wind. Atticus finally got up on his board, pushed twice, and rolled off the ledge with his knees bent, arms out, and Gabriel counted under his breath the whole way down. One one-thousand. Atticus landed in the flat and rolled away, and Gabriel was already writing the number in the margin when Mr. Ba's silver car pulled into the lot.

Mr. Ba taught junior physics and skated badly on Sunday mornings; Gabriel had seen him there before, falling politely. He walked over pushing his own board, looked at the tape measure stretched across the concrete, and raised his eyebrows at the notebook.

"He's verifying your quiz question," Haley said.

"Good," Mr. Ba said. He toed the base of the ledge, glanced at the scuff marks fanned out across the flat, and said nothing else, which Gabriel took as the highest grade the man gave out on weekends.

On Monday Gabriel turned in the corrected problem with the park numbers attached, half a page of measurement and arithmetic, and a last line saying the sideways speed at launch and landing matched within what the stopwatch could resolve. Mr. Ba wrote a small check beside it. He did not write why, and Gabriel noticed, and decided he would keep the why in his pocket as an open question, the way Haley kept a pen behind her ear: not answered, but available. After the bell he found Atticus at the lockers and slid the quiz back through the slats.

"Same speed the whole flight," Gabriel said. "I checked."

"Now you tell me," Atticus said, and shut his locker.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged.
story:
Sadie spread her homework across the kitchen table while her mother washed dishes behind her, the tap running in bursts. On her laptop screen, Nathanael's grid paper filled the camera and Alena's face filled the corner window beneath it.
