Their calculus teacher had posted one problem: find the derivative of the polynomial, then use it to locate the maximum.

"Mine is three x squared minus twelve x," Sadie said. She read it off her page twice to be sure.

"That's wrong," Alena said. "I have three x squared minus twelve x plus seven."

"I wrote what I wrote." Sadie turned her notebook toward the webcam. "Look. Plus zero, I guess. There's no constant on mine."

Nathanael held his paper up. His matched Alena's. "Two against one, Sadie." He was already differentiating his version, pencil moving in short strokes, tongue between his teeth. "So you made the transcription error. That happens when you copy off the board fast."

Sadie didn't answer right away. She reread the function on the whiteboard photo Ms. Lee had posted, zooming in until the pixels blurred. The plus seven was there, plain, attached to the end of the expression, and she had skipped it. Somewhere between the board and her notebook she had dropped a number, and the fact sat in her stomach the way a dropped plate sits on a floor, not yet shattered, only fallen.

Then she differentiated her version anyway, out of a stubbornness she didn't examine. Three x squared minus twelve x became six x minus twelve. She set it equal to zero, solved, and got x equals two. She found the value of the function at two, called out the y-coordinate, and stopped.

"That's my answer," Alena said slowly. "I got x equals two also. And the same y-coordinate. How are we getting the same y-coordinate from different functions?" Her camera flickered as she leaned forward. "One of us has to be wrong somewhere else."

Nathanael, who prided himself on being the trenchant one, the one who cut through confusion, declared that Alena had made an arithmetic slip. "Two functions, two answers. That's just how it works." But he ran his own numbers and got what they got, and the certainty drained out of his voice mid-sentence, which Sadie found more satisfying than she admitted.

She pulled a fresh sheet and sketched two graphs side by side, then on the same axes. One parabola, then a second one floating above it, the same shape translated straight up. Her mother turned off the tap and looked over her shoulder, said something about how it looked like a bowl stacked on a bowl, and went back to the sink. Sadie marked the vertex of each curve. Both sat directly above x equals two. The lower one, the upper one: same x, different heights, and the difference in heights was exactly seven all the way across, she could see it, the gap never pinched and never widened.

"The derivative of a constant is zero," she said. She said it the way you test ice before stepping on it. "So the seven vanishes when you differentiate. Adding seven shifts the whole graph up but leaves the derivative alone." She wrote it in the margin of her notebook, not as an answer, just as something she wanted to keep.

"Then who made the mistake?" Alena asked. "Neither of us? Both of us?"

Sadie ruminate on that while Nathanael argued, with rising volume, that a problem with two different functions couldn't have one answer, that something in the assignment itself must be off. She thought about how Ms. Lee's class ran, its whole milieu of partial credit and check-your-work, and how a mistake in copying had led somewhere more interesting than the correct answer would have. She was honest enough to note what she still didn't know: whether the vertex she'd found was a maximum or a minimum, since the parabola on her page opened upward and the problem had asked for a maximum, and nobody on the call had mentioned it yet.

She flipped her pencil around and shaded the region below each curve.

"Mine opens up," she said. "So this is a minimum, not a maximum. The problem's wrong, or we're solving the wrong thing." She held the page to the camera, one graph, two parabolas, seven units apart, and waited for someone to argue.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll: 200 people out of a 1,000-person sample carry a margin of about plus or minus 7 points.
story:
Justine arrived at the campaign office at nine, before anyone else had thought to unlock the folding chairs, and she stacked them in rows while the coffee machine hissed behind her. She was sixteen and technically too young to canvass alone, but nobody had questioned her after the second week, and she had stopped waiting for permission. The office occupied a rented storefront between a laundromat and a shop that sold tiling, and the smell of both drifted in whenever the door stuck open in the heat.

The problem was the flyer. The candidate, running for a council seat on a promise to fix the flooding on Meridian Street, had approved a mailer that said, in bold letters across the top, YOUNG VOTERS BACK HER 58 TO 42. Justine had been handed the box of them on Tuesday and told to fold, staple, label. She had folded four hundred before she actually read the page.

She found Musa by the copy machine, running off door-hangers, his shirt cuff caught in the tray. She freed it without asking, the way you do when you've known someone since seventh grade.

"Where did the 58 come from?" she asked.

"The poll," Musa said. "The one they paid for. Mr. Do has it on his clipboard."

Mr. Do was the field organizer, a patient man who drank tea instead of coffee and who had once driven forty minutes out of his way to return a wallet one of the volunteers had left in his car. He kept the poll results clipped to a board that he carried everywhere, and when Justine asked to see it, he handed it over without hesitation, which she appreciated, because adults usually asked why first.

The poll had surveyed a thousand people. She found the line for voters under thirty: two hundred of them, and within that group, 58 percent. But at the bottom of the page, in type so small she had to hold the clipboard near the window, she found a note saying that a subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll, and that 200 people out of a 1,000-person sample carry a margin of about plus or minus 7 points.

She read it three times. Then she did the arithmetic on the back of a door-hanger. It could be 51. It could be 65. The whole confident headline sat on a number that could swing seven points in either direction and still be telling the truth about itself.

"The flyer's wrong," she said to Musa.

"It's not wrong," Musa said. "It's what the poll says."

"It's what a slice of the poll says, and the slice is shakier than the whole thing." She showed him the note. He leaned in, squinting, and she watched his expression change from polite to interested, which was the order it always went in with him.

Layan came in at eleven with a bag of bagels for everyone, because she had noticed last week that nobody fed the Saturday volunteers, and she had appointed herself to the task without discussion. She was reading journalism at the college across town and wrote for its paper, and she had come to the office partly to volunteer and partly, Justine suspected, to look for a story. She took a bagel, sat down across from Justine, and pulled one of the folded flyers toward her.

"Where's this from?" Layan asked. Her voice had a new brightness in it.

"The poll they ran," Musa said. "A thousand people."

Layan turned the flyer over, then back. "Young voters breaking 58 to 42," she said slowly. "That's a headline. I could pitch that tonight." She was already pulling out her phone, and Justine could see her drafting the sentence in her head, the way Layan always composed before she typed.

"Wait," Justine said. "How many young people were in it?"

Layan looked up. "Why?"

"Because I think it's two hundred. And two hundred out of a thousand carries a margin of about plus or minus seven points, which is bigger than the margin for the whole poll."

Layan's thumbs stopped. She took the clipboard from Justine and read the small print herself, and the office went quiet enough that they could hear the tiling shop's radio through the wall. Justine watched her face do something complicated, wanting and not wanting the same thing at once.

"So it could be 51 to 49," Layan said. "Or a blowout. I can't headline it either way."

"You could headline the whole poll," Musa offered. "The whole number's solid."

Layan shook her head. "The whole poll isn't news. Everybody already has it." She put the phone face down on the table, which for Layan was a kind of renunciation, and reached for the bag instead.

Justine had expected to feel triumphant. Instead she felt the weight of it, the flyer she still had to fold, the candidate's name on it, the four hundred already labeled in the back room. She thought about her father, who had voted in every election since he became a citizen and who believed numbers the way some people believed weather reports, and she thought about Layan's editor, who would not have read the small print. Two ways of looking at the same page, and neither one wrong exactly, and no way to make them into the same thing. She did not want to dichotomize it into honest people and dishonest people, because the candidate wasn't lying, exactly; she was repeating something a paid pollster had handed her, and the ordinance about campaign mail, whatever it was, surely didn't cover margins.

She went looking for Mr. Do. He was in the back room, wrapping the candidate's yard signs in plastic sheeting against the forecast rain, and when she asked him about the flyers, he set down the roll.

"You folded four hundred before you noticed?" he said.

"I noticed on day one of the rest of them," Justine said. "The four hundred are done. I came about the rest."

He looked at her for a moment in a way that made her feel seen in the specific, perspicacious way he had, not as a volunteer but as someone who had caught something. "It's the campaign's mailer," he said. "It went through the printer before I was consulted."

"Does she know? The candidate."

"I'll call her tonight. She'll want to know, if she's who I think she is." He rubbed his eyes. "You understand we can't afford another poll."

"I'm not asking for one."

He almost smiled. "No. You're asking for something harder."

When she came back out, Layan had written nothing and was instead helping Musa unjam the stapler, her phone still face down, and Justine sat down at the folding table and took a fresh flyer from the box. She folded it, and folded the next, and left the stack of finished ones where the candidate could count them, however she decided to count. Outside, the first of the rain began, soft against the storefront glass, and Layan said, without looking up from the stapler, "Bring me the clipboard again. I want to read the whole thing before I decide what my story is."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
Brayden counted the bills in his pocket twice before he reached the market gate, because twenty-six dollars had to cover a chicken, a bag of carrots, three lemons, and something for dessert, and because counting was easier than thinking about the empty house he would carry it all home to. His mother had left for the night shift at four that morning. His father had left for somewhere else three months ago, and the kitchen, by some unspoken settlement, had become Brayden's territory, the one room nobody fought over.

The farmers' market spread across the closed-off street in white tents, and Brayden moved through it with a list his mother had texted, then a shorter list he had made himself. He stopped at Mr. Banerjee's stall, where the sugar and honey sat in jars with handwritten labels. Mr. Banerjee sold cane sugar in rough golden crystals, and he weighed it slowly, as if the scale were an argument he intended to win.

"It's for caramel sauce," Brayden said. "Over vanilla ice cream."

"Then you will need patience," Mr. Banerjee said, tipping the crystals into a paper bag. "Sugar tells you when it is ready. Most people do not listen."

Trisha found him at the next stall, arguing with a vendor over the last bag of early peaches. She took the bag from his hands, paid for it, and handed it back. "You were going to stand there until he lowered the price, and he wasn't going to. That's not negotiating, that's loitering." She fell into step beside him. "Whose dinner is this?"

"Mine. Mom's on shift. Hamzah's coming at six to eat half of it."

"So you're cooking for a family that isn't home and a friend who is." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she did, and he looked at the peaches instead.

Hamzah arrived at the house before the chicken was out of the oven, kicking the door shut with his backpack still on. He installed himself at the counter with the digital thermometer Brayden had bought with his own money, the one piece of equipment he refused to share. "You know there's a whole argument about how to say caramel," Hamzah said, twisting the probe between his fingers. "Car-mel, two syllables. Or care-a-mel, three. It's basically phonetics. People fight about it."

"Three syllables," Trisha said from the doorway, peaches in her arms.

"It's two," Brayden and Hamzah said together, and for a second the kitchen was easy.

He put the chicken in, set the timer, and then stood at the stove with the sugar and a heavy pan, and this was where the evening turned. He had made caramel sauce once before, at his grandmother's, and it had gone from pale to black in the time it took him to answer a question. He poured the crystals in a flat, even layer over medium heat and watched the edges begin to slacken and shine.

"Here's the thing," Hamzah said, reading off Brayden's phone, which was propped against the flour canister. "Table sugar starts to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius. That's when it browns. That's the actual number."

"Caramelization," Trisha read over his shoulder. "It's the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins. So it's different from when meat browns."

"Then put the probe in," Brayden said.

Hamzah clipped the thermometer to the pan's rim, and they watched the number climb. At 150 the sugar was liquid and clear. At 160 it had gone the color of straw. Trisha leaned in, and Brayden's hand hovered at the pan's handle, and the argument arrived exactly when the sugar did.

"Take it off now," she said. "It's golden. Golden is what you want on ice cream."

"It's not at 170 yet," Brayden said. "If I pull it early it'll just be sweet with no depth. The whole point is that change, the sugar browning on its own, no proteins, nothing else doing the work."

"And if you wait too long it burns, and burnt sugar is genuinely deleterious to the flavor. It's bitter. It tastes like a mistake."

Hamzah held the probe steady and read the temperature out loud, flat as an air traffic controller. 164. 166. The sugar's surface began to darken at the rim, amber deepening toward copper, and the smell shifted from plain sweetness to something richer and almost smoky. Brayden realized he was holding the argument inside himself as much as with Trisha. His father had always taken things off early, chicken still faintly pink at the bone, cautious with everything. His grandmother had let everything go dark and long, certain that the far side of a risk was where the flavor was. He did not want to be either of them tonight. He wanted the number and the color to agree.

At 170 the thermometer chimed, and the sugar turned the color of an old penny in one breath. Brayden lifted the pan off the heat and Trisha had the cream already open, and he poured it in a thin stream while the mixture hissed and boiled up furious and then smoothed. He stirred. The sauce came together glossy and dark amber, and he dipped a spoon and held it out, and Trisha tasted it first.

"Okay," she said. "You were right to wait."

"That's not what I was right about," Brayden said, but he didn't finish the sentence, because the timer went off in a shriek and the oven door needed opening and the peaches needed slicing. Later, when the chicken was carved and the plates were down and Hamzah was already eating, Brayden looked at the pan of cooling caramel and could not say for certain whether the exact moment he chose had been the best one, or only the one the number had permitted him to defend. His mother would taste it cold at midnight. He set a covered dish in the fridge, then took it out, then put it back, and left the spoon resting on top.

"Brayden," Hamzah said, "the ice cream's melting."

Brayden scooped it into three bowls and poured the sauce in a slow spiral over each one.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say, such as anger or love that a line never names out loud.
story:
Ms. Côté had booked the auditorium for Thursday afternoons, all term, and had made each of them sign a form that, in its dense third paragraph, promised to indemnify the school against any injury sustained while constructing sets, a phrase Logan found absurd until he imagined what a collapsing flats-and-two-by-four wall could actually do to a person. He signed it in the second row of the empty auditorium, his knees against the folded seat in front of him, while somewhere above the stage Faye re-rigged a lighting pipe she wasn't supposed to touch.

The assignment was a ten-minute play about a moment from their own lives. "Not your whole life," Ms. Côté had said. "A moment. The smaller the better." Logan had thought immediately of the night his brother came home at two in the morning their father's last week in the house, and the argument that lasted nine minutes by the kitchen clock, and how his brother had left again before the argument was even over. He had written the argument out exactly as he remembered it, all the insults and the slammed door, and it had come out dead on the page, like a transcript of a hearing nobody attended.

He sat on the apron of the stage now with Sloane, who was reading it for the third time and frowning at the same page each time. "It's all out loud," she said finally. "Everything they feel, they say. It's like they're narrating their own fight."

"That's how it happened, though."

"Okay." She handed the pages back. "But when your brother says 'You always take his side,' what's he actually feeling?"

Logan didn't answer, because the answer was obvious and he didn't want it in the room yet. Faye climbed down from the scaffold and dropped onto the stage beside them, unscrewing a gobo from a lighting instrument with a socket wrench, and said, without looking up, "Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say. Like anger or love that a line never names out loud." She said it the way she said most things, dry and certain, as though reading off an inventory sheet. "My cousin's a stage manager. She says it constantly."

"You're being facetious," Logan said.

"I'm never facetious about lighting." But she was smiling at the gobo.

He took the pages home and worked on them at the kitchen table where the actual argument had happened, which he understood was a dramatic choice in itself, though not one he'd made on purpose. He cut every line that named a feeling. Where his brother had said "I can't stand being in this house," the character now said, "Is there any of that coffee left." Where his father had said "You're tearing this family apart," he said nothing at all, just stood and washed the two mugs that were already clean. The fight in the revised draft was about the coffee, about who had moved the car keys, about a porch light left burning all night, and it was somehow much worse to read than the version with the shouting. He read it twice and then set it face down on the table.

At Thursday's workshop, the class read it aloud in the dusty gold of the work lights, and by the fourth page the room had gone quiet in a way Logan could feel in his own throat. Afterward a girl from his chemistry class said, "Wait, so the brother wants to be forgiven? He never says that." And Sloane said, "He doesn't have to," and looked at Logan in a way that suggested she understood exactly which real person the brother was, though she'd never met him and never would, since the real brother now lived four hours north and called on Sundays.

He staged it in the auditorium with two chairs and the coffee table hauled up from the green room. He played the father, which he had not planned; the boy who was supposed to read the part was absent, and Logan stood up from the folding seats before anyone else could. Saying the father's small lines, the ones about the mugs and the porch light, he found he could hear his own father's cadence in them, and he understood something he couldn't yet put in words: that his memory of the argument had been wrong in an ordinary way. Everyone had been lying that night, and the lies were the record. He had spent months assembling the wrong evidence, the shouted sentences, when the truth had been in the pauses, which no one had thought to write down.

His brother came to the performance. This was the part Logan hadn't arranged, though his mother had, and she sat in the third row with her coat still on. When the lights came up, his brother was in the back row with his hands folded, and during the scene about the car keys he laughed once, quietly, at a line Logan had taken verbatim from the real night, and Logan heard it across the whole auditorium. Afterward, in the lobby with its trophy case and its smell of floor wax, his brother shook his hand as though they'd just met, formally, and said, "It didn't happen like that."

"It did," Logan said.

"No." His brother looked back toward the stage, where Faye was already striking the chairs. "He said sorry. Right at the end, after I left. Mom told you that, didn't she?" And he waited, in the doorway, for an answer that Logan, who had written the whole fight and left the sorry out, could not give him.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
story:
The rink closed for a private party at half past eight, which gave Loic exactly one hour, and he had already spent six minutes of it standing at the skate rental counter pretending to study the blade of a size ten.

Abby arrived at seven minutes past, hair still damp from a shower she had evidently rushed through, and slid her own skates across the counter to Mr. Haddad, who sharpened them on Thursday afternoons and kept them behind the register for her. She had been coming to this rink since she was seven. Loic had been coming since September, which was one of the many asymmetries he tried not to think about.

"You're early," she said.

"I didn't want to be late."

"That's the same thing as being early, just sadder." She laced her skates faster than he did, sitting on the bench with one ankle crossed over the other, and when he glanced up again he found he was sitting with one ankle crossed over the other. He uncrossed it. Then, feeling that uncrossing it was somehow ruder than having crossed it, he crossed it again.

He had read something, weeks ago, in a psychology book his mother had left in the bathroom: in a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. It had struck him as both sleazy and hopeful, depending on who was doing it. Since then he had caught himself cataloguing it everywhere, in the way Alden and his lab partner fell into the same slump over their shared textbook, in the way the coach folded his arms and the whole bench folded theirs. He could not decide whether it meant people were transparent or generous, and he had not expected the question to become urgent tonight, on ice, of all places, where posture was mostly a matter of not dying.

They skated the slow oval at the rink's edge. The public session thinned as families left for dinner, and the music got older, and Abby told a story about a physics test that Loic mostly followed. Twice she leaned on the boards, elbows out, chin on her fists, and twice he found his own elbows sliding along the rail until the pose matched hers, at which point his whole awareness collapsed into his shoulders. He tried to be natural about it. There was no natural way to be natural about it.

"Your crossovers are better," she said as they rounded the far turn. "You've been holding back, I've seen you at practice with Alden. You skate like you're apologizing to the ice."

"That's my whole phenomenology," he said. "The world as it appears to an apologizing sixteen-year-old."

She laughed, which he was sanguine enough to count as a point in his favor, and then, without warning, she stopped at the boards and looked at him rather than at the ice, which was a look he did not have a script for. The Zamboni driver was unlocking the gate across the rink. It was eight twenty-two.

"Can I tell you something without it making things weird," she said, "or should I extenuate it first, drag in all the circumstances so you can't be mad?"

"You can't say a sentence like that and then pause."

She pulled off one glove, finger by finger. "I'm moving Sunday. My mom's job, the one in Ohio she interviewed for in October. We found out last week. I didn't tell you because I wanted tonight to happen at all, and I thought if I told you, you'd make it into a goodbye instead of a date."

The word date sat there on the cold air. So she had known it was one. He opened his mouth to say something forgiving and generous, the kind of thing a person says when he has been handed a good exit, and instead he heard himself saying, "I've been copying you. Your posture. On the bench, at the rail. There was this study, 1999, these researchers, Chartrand and Bargh, they found people like a partner more when the partner mimics their gestures, even without noticing it. I read it in a book and I couldn't stop thinking about it and apparently I couldn't stop doing it either, and I don't even know if I was doing it on purpose."

Abby stared at him. Then she put her glove back on, very deliberately, and leaned her elbows on the boards, chin on her fists, and waited. The Zamboni rumbled out onto the far end of the ice, laying down its clean sheet.

"Well?" she said. "The rink's closing in six minutes. Catch up."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage.
story:
The listing said 11:00 sharp, so Evan's mother made them arrive at 10:50, which left them standing in a stairwell that smelled of cabbage and floor wax while a woman named Ms. Kerr, the building manager, jangled through an enormous ring of keys. Evan had his phone out, doing math. Two bedrooms, $1,850 a month, first month plus last month plus a security deposit equal to one month's rent. He added it in his head twice and got $5,550 both times, a number that seemed to belong to a different family than theirs.

"You'll want to see the light in the afternoon," Ms. Kerr said, pushing open the door. "Afternoon is when this place shows itself."

The apartment was bigger than he expected and older than the photos. His mother walked the perimeter the way she inspected everything, touching the radiator, lifting a corner of the blind, asking about utilities, about parking, about whether the deposit was refundable. Evan hung back near the window. Below, in the courtyard, an old woman was sweeping leaves off a bench with her hand, unhurried, though the wind kept undoing her work.

"Deposit's refundable," Ms. Kerr said. "Minus damages, obviously. You break it, you buy it, that's the whole arrangement. And rent's due on the first, grace period till the third, after that late fee."

His mother nodded and wrote nothing down, which Evan knew was a performance for him, a show of calm. Two years ago she'd have written everything down. He watched her ask whether the landlord would consider a twelve-month lease at a slightly lower rate, and Ms. Kerr said landlords rarely considered anything, and his mother laughed a laugh that had no air in it.

There was a question Evan couldn't make himself ask, which was why they were here at all. His mother had said only, "Come with me Saturday, I want your eyes," and his grandmother's car had not been in its driveway when they passed it, and his grandmother was supposed to be at the viewing too, she'd said so Thursday on the phone, and she was not here. He kept that fact folded small in his chest while he followed the women from room to room.

His grandmother arrived at last, twenty minutes late, apologizing to nobody in particular, smelling of the cold. She hugged Evan hard enough that he felt her coat buttons. "So this is it," she said. "This is what $1,850 buys." She said it without judgment, almost fondly, and then to his mother, low, by the kitchen door: "The buyer's inspection went through. We close on the twelfth." His mother's shoulders changed shape. Evan pretended to study the oven.

"You're selling the house," he said to his grandmother later, when his mother and Ms. Kerr had gone down to sign something about the waiting list. They sat on the steps outside, and the old woman from the courtyard was gone, the bench empty, the leaves already reclaiming it.

"I've sold it," she said. "And I did well, because of equity. Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage." She said it briskly, like reciting a recipe, then looked at him to see if he'd caught it. He ran it backward. Her house had been paid off for years, which meant nothing was still owed, which meant the whole current value was hers to keep. Her neighbor on the left, she mentioned, the one with the flag, had refinanced twice and would walk away from a sale with barely a tenth of what she would. Same street, same market, entirely different exits. The word equity had always floated past him in commercials, attached to smiling couples, and now it had edges.

"So the house money is the deposit," he said slowly, testing whether the thought was tenable, whether it could hold weight. "For here. First, last, security. That's why we're viewing it."

"Some of it," his grandmother said. "Your mother wouldn't take all of it. We argued about the proportion for two days and then I stopped arguing, because she predicates everything on not being a burden to me, and you cannot argue a person out of a value, you can only tire them." She rubbed her hands together for warmth. "I told her she was ridiculous. She told me I was stubborn. Both statements were accurate."

Evan thought of his mother downstairs, signing the waiting list form, and of the way she'd laughed in the kitchen, and he understood that he had spent the whole morning doing arithmetic on the wrong thing. He had been adding up $5,550 like it was a wall between them and this apartment, when the actual wall was something his mother would rather pay twice than admit existed. He still didn't know how much his grandmother had given, or how much was left, or what would happen if his mother's hours at the clinic got cut again. Those stayed open, like the lease, like everything.

His mother came out the lobby door with a carbon copy of a form held against the wind. "We're fourth on the list," she said. "The agent says a unit opens up in March."

"March," his grandmother repeated, and stood, and pulled her coat tighter, and looked up at the third-floor windows of the apartment they probably would not get.

"Then we'd better keep looking," she said, and started toward the car.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration states that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures.
story:
Ms. Esposito set the photocopy face-down on Sara's desk like a card she wasn't ready to turn over. "Your side speaks first on Thursday," she said. "Petition to suspend the county's new mosquito pesticide pending further study. You're for the suspension." The classroom smelled of wet jackets and radiator dust, and outside the window the October light was already thinning at three in the afternoon.

Sara had wanted the other side. She had spent the weekend pulling sources that made suspension look reckless, whole paragraphs about West Nile cases in the next county over, and now she would have to argue against her own preparation. She found Sasha by the lockers and complained about it, and Sasha only laughed. "That's the assignment," Sasha said. "You get handed a position and you build the case. That's what lawyers do." But it didn't feel like a costume to Sara. It felt like being asked to hold something she wasn't sure she could carry.

The county had started spraying in August, after two dead crows tested positive. The pesticide was new enough that the label still felt like a rumor, old enough that nobody in Sara's town could remember voting on anything. By late September the bees around the community garden were fewer, though the beekeeper who kept the hives was also seventy-six and had stopped keeping careful records, which meant the decline proved nothing, which meant it could be used to prove anything.

Sara went to the library on Tuesday with a legal pad and the presentiment, vague but persistent, that the argument she needed was not the one she was looking for. She had expected to find studies. What she found instead, three pages into a United Nations document from 1992 called the Rio Declaration, was a single principle that seemed to have been written for exactly this moment, though it had been written thirty years before it. She copied it onto the pad in her fastest handwriting, then copied it again more slowly, because the first version had skipped a word.

"Did you find anything?" Ethan asked on Wednesday. He was arguing the other side, and they had agreed to trade sources, a pact that both of them suspected the other of not fully honoring. Ethan slid a folder across the lab table: printouts about larvicide alternatives, cost estimates, a quote from a county health officer. Sara slid her own folder back and watched his face as he read the page she had put on top.

"Principle 15," Ethan said. "Of the Rio Declaration." He read it aloud under his breath, and Sara heard it the way she had that afternoon in the library. "Where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures." He looked up. "So you're saying we don't wait for proof."

"That's what it says." Sara kept her voice level. "It's called the precautionary principle." Ethan was quiet for a moment, turning his pencil over. "But suspending the spray is a preventive measure too," he said. "You're preventing the county from protecting people. Every principle cuts both ways if you hold it right." It was an annoying thing to say and also a true thing, and Sara wrote it down on her legal pad under the principle itself.

She spent that evening acclimating to the argument the way you acclimate to cold water, one disagreeable fact at a time. Her mother asked from the kitchen whether she wanted dinner, and Sara said in a minute, and then sat for forty minutes longer with the pad. If she argued for suspension, she was arguing that a possible harm to bees and gardens outweighed a documented harm to people two counties away. If she argued against it, she was saying that irreversible damage was acceptable so long as it hadn't been proven. Somewhere between those two positions was the actual question, and it did not fit on either side of a debate.

Thursday came gray and colder. The classroom had been rearranged into two facing rows, and Ms. Esposito sat at the side with a timer and a legal pad of her own. Ethan opened with the crows, the case counts, the numbers of the thing, and he was good, confident without being slick. When Sara's turn came she stood, and the room was quieter than she expected.

"My opponent wants proof of harm before we act," she said. "Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration says that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures." She paused, because the next part was the part she had rewritten four times. "But I want to be honest about what that doesn't settle. Suspension is also a preventive measure, and it has costs that fall on people who can't choose them. The principle tells us not to wait for certainty. It doesn't tell us whose uncertainty matters more."

Ethan leaned forward. "So which is it?" he said, and half the row behind him laughed, and Ms. Esposito didn't stop it, because it was a fair question. Sara looked down at her legal pad, at the principle in her own handwriting, at Ethan's line beneath it about principles cutting both ways. "I'm getting to that," she said, and turned the page over.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Nathan had spread the papers across a folding table beside the shallow end, where the smell of chlorine sat heavy in the August heat. The sheets were his father's old training plan, laminated and curling at the corners, rescued from a box in the garage after Nathan announced he would run cross-country in the fall. Across the top, in faded marker, someone had written the words he had repeated to himself all week like a law: 10 percent, no more. Never raise your weekly mileage more than ten percent. The rule had a reassuring arithmetic to it, and Nathan liked arithmetic. It promised that discipline could be counted.

Larissa arrived with her towel over one shoulder and dropped into the chair across from him, dripping on his spreadsheets. She was here for the evening lap swim, but she had a way of inserting herself into other people's projects as though they were communal property. "You're doing homework at the pool," she said. "That's a new low, even for you."

"It's a season plan." He turned the pages toward her. "Eighteen weeks, building from twenty miles. Every week adds exactly ten percent, and every fourth week drops back for rest. Warm-up drills on Tuesdays, strides on Saturdays."

She squinted at the columns, then at him, and he could see her deciding whether to say the thing she was already saying. "My sister's in physio school. She calls that the ten percent rule. Never raise your weekly distance more than ten percent." She flicked the corner of the page. "She also says studies haven't shown it prevents injuries any better than other gradual plans."

Nathan felt something in him resist, the way a swimmer resists cold water on the first plunge. A rule was supposed to be load-bearing. He wanted to believe that if he followed it exactly, his shins would owe him their loyalty, that the numbers would burnish the plan into something unbreakable. "Then what does prevent injuries?" he asked.

"Gradual stuff. Which you're doing anyway." She stood, hitched her goggles. "You might be worshipping the wrong god, is all I'm saying."

He sat there after she dove in, listening to the muffled churn of the lap lanes, and pulled out his phone. He read for twenty minutes, then thirty, scrolling past forums where runners argued about the rule with the fervor of creditors at an insolvency hearing, each certain the other was bankrupt of evidence. The studies were messier than the rule. Some found no clear benefit over other sensible progressions. One had even tracked runners who followed it strictly and been hurt anyway. Nobody had proven it wrong, exactly. Nobody had proven it right.

The trouble was that his father had followed it. Nathan remembered being nine, waiting at the kitchen table with a grilled cheese going cold, while his father stood at the counter with the same laminated sheets, marking off weeks with a grease pencil. He remembered the walking boot the following October, and the way his father had said the rule was supposed to prevent this, as if the rule had personally betrayed him. Nathan had always assumed his father had broken it somehow. He had never once considered that the rule itself might have been a coin flip dressed up as a guarantee.

Rhiannon surfaced near the table, out of breath from her set, shaking water from her ears. She was the fastest girl on the team and famously indifferent to planning; she trained, as she put it, by vibes. "Ms. Hu says you're the one organizing the summer mileage group," she said. "Count me in. But I'm only doing the days I feel good."

"That's not a plan, that's a mood."

"Your plan is a mood too. You just feel good about spreadsheets." She grinned and pushed off the wall again before he could argue.

He gathered the papers slowly, watching the long evening light lie flat and orange on the water, thinking about Ms. Hu, who had watched him arrange the pages and said only that a plan should leave room for the days a body says no. Maybe that was the honest position: gradual was the real principle, and the ten percent was one way of being gradual, no better proven than others. He could keep the structure, the rest weeks, the drills, and hold the sacred number more loosely, admitting which parts were knowledge and which were ritual.

His father answered on the second ring. "Hey. Found the training sheets, huh."

"I found them." Nathan watched Larissa turn at the far wall, sleek and unhurried. "Did you follow it? That fall. The whole thing, exactly?"

There was a pause long enough for a swimmer to cross the pool. "Every week," his father said. "To the decimal."

Nathan looked down at the laminated page, at the grease pencil marks still faintly visible in the margins, week eleven circled twice. He slid the sheets back into his bag and zipped it shut.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Lynn Hunt's 1984 book Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources for understanding the Revolution.
story:
The essay prompt had been sitting in Rachel's bag for five days before she finally read it at her grandmother's kitchen table, between a plate of arrowroot biscuits and a crossword her grandfather had abandoned half-finished. Historiography, Ms. Janssen had written on the sheet, is not the past itself but the story of how the past has been told. Trace how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800, and take a position on which account you find most convincing, and why. Rachel read it three times, then ate a biscuit, then felt the particular dread of a task that could not be solved by memorizing dates.

She had been sent to her grandparents' house for the week while her parents were away, and she had brought the prompt the way one brings a toothbrush, out of obligation rather than intention. Her grandfather, retired from teaching history at the community college, occupied the armchair by the window with a paperback folded against his knee. When she asked him what historians used to say about the Revolution, he waved a hand toward the hall. "Third shelf," he said. "I haven't thought about that in years. Look for yourself."

The third shelf held books with cracked spines and marginalia in three different pens. She pulled down a survey from the 1960s that called the Revolution the triumph of a rising middle class, then a thinner one from the 1970s that treated it as a social crisis, then a fat green volume she nearly missed because it had fallen sideways behind the others. Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution, by Lynn Hunt, 1984. The date stopped her. Everything else on the shelf was older and grimmer, and this one, when she flipped it open, had a plate of a festival print inside, citizens dancing around a liberty tree, and whole chapters on language and symbols. She carried it back to the kitchen.

"Grandpa, this one's different. It talks about festivals. Revolutionary festivals, like they were important."

He put his paperback face-down on the armrest. "That book," he said. "Lynn Hunt's. 1984. It turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources for understanding the Revolution." He said it slowly, the way he recited things he had once lectured about, and Rachel wrote the sentence in her notebook word for word, because it sounded like the hinge the whole assignment was turning on.

That evening Eunice cycled over, ostensibly to study for chemistry, actually to eat the biscuits and complain about Ms. Janssen. "I'm just going to argue that the Revolution was good," Eunice said. "Bread and equality. Done."

"You can't. It's not asking what happened. It's asking what people thought happened, and when." Rachel showed her the green book, open to the festival print. Eunice leaned in, chewing. In the image, a woman in flowing robes held a pike topped with a cap, and ordinary citizens in the background looked up at her with their hats off. "That's decoration," Eunice said. "They put a lady on it so people would look."

But Rachel kept returning to the print after Eunice had gone back to her ions. If people in 1793 needed a woman in robes to look at, that told her something about what they wanted, the way the posters in the school hallway about the food drive told her what the school wanted to believe about itself. Evidently Hunt had thought so too, an entire chapter on the political vocabulary of the Revolution, words like citizen and nation remade and reused. Rachel, who had habituated herself to thinking of evidence as numbers of harvest failures and tax rolls, sat with the unfamiliar idea that an image could carry weight in an argument. She texted Camden, who was doing the same essay in the other class.

Camden texted back a photo of his outline, which was four points long and ended with "therefore, Napoleon was inevitable." Beneath it he typed: is there even a right answer. She typed "probably not" and then deleted it, because it felt like surrender, and typed instead: there are better and worse ones. She stared at that for a while. The old books on the shelf had been confident, each in its decade, and each confidence had been quietly replaced. Her grandfather, she remembered suddenly, had once told her mother that he'd left the college because the department couldn't agree on what the discipline was for, a memory that surfaced now with an equivocal weight she couldn't settle, pride or disappointment or both.

In the morning he found her at the table with the Hunt book and her notebook, the festival print propped against the sugar bowl. "You've got the phylogeny of it now," he said, tapping the shelf. "One line descending from another. Nineteenth-century liberals, then the social school, then her." He poured his coffee. "The trouble with the family tree is deciding which branch you live on."

Rachel spent the afternoon drafting, crossing out, drafting again. Her opening paragraph compared the 1960s survey's certainty about class with Hunt's attention to symbols, and her position, when she finally wrote it, was less a verdict than a leaning: the social historians explained why the Revolution happened, and Hunt's approach explained what it meant to the people living through it, and she could not see how to choose one without losing the other. She wrote an honest sentence at the bottom of the page saying so, and did not delete it.

She read the draft aloud to her grandfather before bed, stumbling once over "historiographical," and when she finished he was quiet for long enough that she checked his face. He was looking past her at the shelf. "Your grandmother gave me that book," he said. "1985. I told her at the time I thought it was a passing fashion." He picked up his pen and reached for the abandoned crossword. "Six letters, third one an A, 'festival'."

"FIESTA," Rachel said.

"Fête," he said, and began writing.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
The lanterns had been strung across the community hall ceiling in loops of red and gold, and Hannah watched her little cousin stand beneath them, mouth open, mesmerized by the light the way she herself must have been at that age, before she learned to check her phone under the table. The hall smelled of fried dumplings and orange peel. Folding tables lined the walls, and at the far end her grandmother was presiding over the tea like a small emperor, which was fitting, since it was her insistence that had gotten everyone here on a Saturday afternoon in the first place.

Hannah's job was the red envelopes. Her aunt had handed her a stack of them, crisp and slit at the top, plus a shoebox of new bills, and told her to fill one for each cousin under sixteen. This was meant as an honor, Hannah understood, and also as a test, though her aunt would never say the word test out loud. She would just watch, over her shoulder, with the mild smile of a woman grading silently.

She had done eleven envelopes, eight dollars each, when Iris arrived, pink-nosed from the cold and carrying a plastic bag of mandarins as tribute. "I brought fruit," Iris announced, "because I googled it and fruit seemed safe." Jaeden came in behind her, still in his soccer jacket, there only because his mother had traded him two hours of hall-duty for the promise of leftovers.

"Cash," Jaeden said, looking into the shoebox with reverence. "You're literally counting money at a party. This is my dream job."

"It's not a job, it's a tradition," Hannah said, and heard, even as she said it, how much like her grandmother she sounded.

Her youngest cousin, seven and missing a front tooth, had appointed herself Hannah's assistant and was now stuffing envelopes with the concentration of a surgeon. Hannah turned to shoo Iris toward the dumpling table, and when she looked back, the girl had laid two bills into the next envelope, smooth side up, very proud.

Two twenties. Forty dollars, which was wildly over budget and, more importantly, exactly wrong.

"Wait, not that one." Hannah put her hand over the envelope before she had fully decided what to say. The trouble was that she knew the shape of the rule without being sure she could stand behind it; her grandmother had mentioned it once, years ago, in passing, the way she mentioned most things, and Hannah had filed it away without checking the file. "You can't do forty. Take one of these back."

"Why not?" said her cousin, wounded. "It's more money. More is better. That's just math."

Before Hannah could answer, Iris leaned in, peering at the red paper. "Is there a thing with the amount? There's a thing with the amount, isn't there."

"Eight is good," Hannah said slowly, working it out as she said it, testing each word against what she remembered. "Forty's not. In Chinese, the word for four sounds like the word for death." Her cousin's eyes went wide and delighted, the way children's eyes do at anything grim. "So you don't put four in a lucky envelope. It would be like handing someone a card that says congratulations on your death."

"That's the best thing I've ever heard," Jaeden said. "I'm putting three dollars in everything from now on. No wait. Four dollars. To my enemies."

"There's nobody to give envelopes to, you don't have enemies," said Iris.

"I could develop some."

Hannah swapped the twenty for a single, then had to sit with the small strange feeling that she had, for once, been the person in the family who knew the thing. Usually it went the other way. Usually she was the one standing at the edge of a conversation in two languages, catching every third brick of it. Her aunt drifted past, ostensibly to refill the teapot, and glanced at the envelope pile, and Hannah saw her count the bills in the box, and then look at the seven-year-old, who was now cheerfully telling anyone within range that she had almost given somebody death money.

Her aunt's face went through several seasons. It settled, at last, on something like clemency.

"She caught it," the aunt said to her grandmother, in Cantonese, not knowing, or perhaps forgetting, or perhaps not caring, that Hannah could follow. "The little one was putting in forty."

"I know," Hannah said, in English, and then, because her grandmother's eyebrows had risen a full centimeter, in Cantonese, "I stopped her."

The hall went quiet in the way it does when a room full of people pretends it wasn't listening. Ms. MacLeod, the neighbor who had the key to the hall and had stayed for the dumplings, looked up from her tea with the expression of a woman who had watched four acts of a play and was missing the fifth.

Her grandmother said nothing for a long moment. Then she reached into her cardigan pocket, took out one last red envelope, and held it out across the table, flat on her palm, like a card dealer or a queen.

"For the girl who remembers," she said. Then, to the seven-year-old, who had already begun to dance: "You. Sit down. You are still on probation."

"Hannah gets an envelope and I don't even get a dumpling," Jaeden said to Iris. "Explain the system to me again."

"Lucky money brings luck," Iris said solemnly. "That's why it's lucky."

"That's tautological," said Jaeden.

Hannah took the envelope, and did not open it, and put it in the inner pocket of her jacket where it made a small square shape against her ribs, and went back to counting eights.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Some leases require the tenant to carry renter's insurance, which covers the tenant's own belongings rather than the building and adds a monthly premium.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and free coffee, which Vincent considered a fair trade, since he had come to make the biggest financial decision of his sixteen years. He spread two leases across the little desk by the waiting area, aligning their corners like a man setting up a chess board. Katia dropped into the chair across from him with a slushie the approximate size of her head.

"You brought paperwork to a bank," she said. "Voluntarily. On a Saturday."

"I brought organization to chaos." He tapped the first page. "Apartment A, six blocks from campus, seven fifty a month. Apartment B, four blocks, eight hundred. Utilities included at B, not at A. That's the whole decision, right? Wrong. Nothing is ever the whole decision."

Katia peered at the pages as though they might bite. "This is the apartment your mom's co-signing? The one you've been maligning all week because the landlord's email signature is a Comic Sans flamingo?"

"It's a point against him. Character matters in a lease." Vincent flattened the second lease with his palm. "Here's my problem. I added everything up. At A, with utilities estimated at ninety a month, I get eight hundred forty total. At B, all-inclusive, eight hundred. B wins by forty dollars. That's two slushies. But my budget only stretches to eight twenty-five, so if I'm wrong by even a little, I'm looking at personal insolvency by October. Which is a fancy word for eating my roommate's leftovers without asking."

"Your budget is forty dollars of margarine," Katia said solemnly.

"My budget is forty dollars of hope." He slid his finger down the fine print of lease A, the part he'd skimmed three times and meant to skim a fourth, when a clause snagged him like a hook. Section 12, Subsection C. Tenant shall carry renter's insurance for the term of the lease, proof of which must be provided prior to occupancy.

"Katia. Katia, look at this."

"Is it the flamingo?"

"Lease A requires renter's insurance." He said the words aloud, twice, testing them. "I don't have that. I don't know what that costs. It's a monthly thing, it has to be a monthly thing, which means my eight forty isn't eight forty, it's eight forty plus something, and my whole spreadsheet just fell off a cliff."

Mr. Hughes, the advisor whose desk was nearest and who had clearly been eavesdropping with the gentle patience of a man who had heard many spreadsheets fall off many cliffs, rolled his chair over. "Renter's insurance? Couple of my student clients carry it. Covers your own belongings, not the building itself. The landlord's policy handles the building. Yours handles your stuff. Adds a premium to your monthly costs, usually not enormous, but it's a premium, it's monthly, and it's yours to pay."

"So it's like the lease makes me insure my own furniture," Vincent said slowly.

"Your own everything," Mr. Hughes said. "Your laptop, your guitar, whatever you'd cry about in a fire."

Vincent flipped to lease B, the flamingo lease, and hunted through its fine print with the urgency of a man checking a lottery ticket. No insurance clause. None. B was eight hundred, all-inclusive, no hidden rider, no additional premium, no fifth line item he hadn't budgeted. He sat back.

"The Comic Sans flamingo man," he said, "is forty dollars cheaper than I thought, and the sensible Helvetica person is more expensive than I thought. I've been maligning the wrong landlord this entire time. I owe him an apology. Or at least a strongly worded thank-you."

"To be fair," Katia said, "the flamingo is unforgivable on its own terms."

"It is. But it's unforgivable and affordable." Vincent pulled his notebook over and redid the arithmetic, and here he paused, because the numbers did something he hadn't expected: they came out nearly even. If the insurance premium was small, A might still beat B on price. If it wasn't, B won outright. He didn't know yet which it was. He wrote both totals, one in each column, and underlined neither.

"Here's the thing," he said. "I came in thinking this was a math problem with one answer. It's a math problem with two answers, and the answer depends on a number I don't have until I call an insurance company on Monday. The eight-forty could be eight-sixty. It could be eight-fifty-five. I can't know today."

"So what do you do today?"

"Today I decide what I'm willing to risk." He tapped the columns. "B is certain. Eight hundred, done, flamingo and all. A is a gamble on a phone call. And I'm seventeen dollars an hour at the garden center, so a gamble I get wrong costs me a weekend of wheelbarrows." He looked at the pages a long moment, then turned them toward Katia. "Be honest. If you were me."

Katia slurped the last of her slushie with tremendous ceremony. "I'm not you. I'm famously not altruistic, I don't even share fries. But if I were you, I'd take the certain thing, and I'd frame the flamingo email as a souvenir."

Vincent laughed, stacked the two leases, and squared their edges on the desk. Then he took out his phone and, before he could think better of it, began drafting the message to the flamingo man, starting with the words "I'd like to apply for."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do.
story:
Christopher had drilled the bay park until he could do it half asleep, reversing into the painted lines of the supermarket car park on Ashfield Road with a smoothness that almost bored him, and it was exactly that smoothness, he realized the night before his test, that might undo him. He was in his father's garage, which smelled of engine oil and the damp cardboard of old boxes, sitting on an upturned crate with the highway code open on his knees and his phone torch angled across the page. Bay parking was one thing. But on the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road was one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner might ask a candidate to do, and the examiner did not have to warn you which one was coming.

Braiden sat on the workbench, heels drumming against the cupboard below, eating crisps from a share bag he had no intention of sharing. "You've done bays for three months," he said. "You'll be fine."

"That's the problem. Three months of one thing isn't practice, it's a groove." Christopher turned the page. "If he asks for a parallel park, I've done it maybe four times, all last autumn."

"So do it a few more times before tomorrow."

"Where? It's dark, and Mum's car is insured for lessons with the instructor, not for me messing about at midnight."

Braiden crumpled the bag and looked around the garage as though the solution were shelved beside the spanners. What he found instead was Mariane, who appeared at the side door in her running gear, breathing hard, having seen the light from the street. She was the only one of them who had already passed, back in March, first attempt.

"I heard you panicking from the pavement," she said. "It carries."

"I'm not panicking. I'm being realistic."

"Those are the same thing at eleven at night." She came in, pulled the crate out from under him, and sat. "Okay. Tell me what happens in a parallel park. Not the steering, the observation."

He tried it, haltingly. Reference point at the parked car's door pillar, full lock, watch for the corner of the kerb in the left mirror, straighten, ease back. The words came out in his father's cadences, learned from the passenger seat, and he heard for the first time how secondhand they were, how he had repeated them without ever assembling them into something he owned.

"You're reciting," Mariane said, not unkindly. "Reciting gets people through bays. Bays forgive you. A road doesn't, because the road has traffic in it." She had, she admitted, been terrified of the parallel park herself, so terrified that she had asked her instructor for an extra hour on nothing else, and then the examiner had asked her for a bay park and she had nearly botched it from sheer surprise. "The trick isn't knowing one manoeuvre," she said. "It's knowing that either one might come, and being okay with that."

Braiden, who had gone quiet, said, "So what do we actually do? He can't practise a road in a garage."

Mariane stood and walked the length of the concrete floor, from the rolled door to the far wall, counting under her breath. Then she dragged the crate to the middle of the space, fetched a second one, and set the two of them side by side near the wall with a gap between them about the length of a car. "That's your parked car," she said, pointing at the first crate. "That's the kerb, more or less. You walk it. Every step, you tell us what you'd be seeing."

So he walked it, at first clumsily, mouthing mirror checks at a wall that held no mirror, and it felt ridiculous, and Braiden laughed, and then Braiden stopped laughing and started asking questions instead: what about a cyclist coming up on the left, what if the gap was tight, what if the examiner tapped the sheet early. By the third circuit Christopher was no longer reciting his father's script. He was noticing that his version of the manoeuvre had assumptions baked into it, a certain width of road, a certain patience in the traffic behind him, and one by one he named those assumptions and let them go, replacing them with what Mariane had said about readiness rather than rehearsal. The two ways of thinking sat side by side in him, the drilled certainty of the bay park and the looser, wider watchfulness she was describing, and neither erased the other. He could not yet say which one would matter tomorrow, and he was honest with himself about that: the uncertainty did not dissolve just because he had walked a garage floor in circles.

At half past eleven his mother's key scraped in the front door and her voice came through the wall, asking why the garage light was on. Mariane gathered her jacket. "One more thing," she said at the side door, the night air cold behind her. "If he asks for the parallel park, he's not trying to catch you out. He just might ask for it. That's all it is." She squeezed his shoulder, a gesture so brief it was almost evanescent, and then she was gone down the drive.

Braiden lingered, wiping crisp salt off his hands onto his jeans. "You know you've become, like, a connoisseur of parking theory," he said. "That's not a compliment."

"It's a little bit of a compliment."

"It's not." Braiden grinned and pulled the rolled door down for him, the metal rattling into its groove. "Text me after. Even if you fail."

"Especially if I fail."

"Especially then." The door thumped shut, and through the gap at the bottom Christopher watched Braiden's trainers cross the wet pavement, then stop, then turn back, and a hand appeared under the door with a thumbs up.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The overall equation for aerobic cellular respiration is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy: glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water.
story:
Jessica had the whole backyard to herself, which was how she liked it, and she spread her notes across the picnic table as if she were laying out evidence in a case she had already solved. She hadn't solved it. She was failing biology in the specific way where she understood every word and none of the sentences, but she had told Angelie she was basically fine, and she had almost told Petra the same thing before Petra started talking about her own grade, and so the lie had hardened into a kind of veneer, smooth on the outside, with the mess sealed underneath.

The unit test was Monday. On the table in front of her, her notes said, in her own handwriting: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water. She'd copied it off the board without thinking, the way you copy a phone number you intend to memorize later and never do.

"You're out here rotting in the sun," Angelie said, coming through the gate with two iced teas and no announcement, as usual. She set one down on the corner of Jessica's notes, where the condensation immediately bloomed a ring through the word mitochondria.

"I'm studying."

"You're staring."

These were, Jessica had to admit, both true, though she chose to be annoyed about the second one. Angelie dropped onto the bench across from her and pulled a grape from the bag she'd brought, and behind her, at the far edge of the yard, the little pond her father had dug three summers ago sat green and still. A dragonfly stitched over it. Jessica looked at the pond, then at her equation, then at the pond again.

"Can I ask you something stupid," Jessica said.

"Those are the only ones you ask."

"Where does the carbon in your breath come from? When you breathe out carbon dioxide. The carbon part."

Angelie chewed the grape slowly, in the way she did when she was deciding whether to be smart or funny. "From you, I guess. From food. From the grape." She held up the stem as evidence. "Wait, is that right?"

Jessica looked at the equation again. Glucose. C6H12O6. Six carbons, sitting right there in the formula she'd copied without understanding, and then on the other side of the arrow, six carbon dioxides. She felt the way she did when a word she'd read a hundred times suddenly sounds like itself. The carbon went in one end, attached to oxygen, and came out the other. It wasn't created in her lungs. It was passed through, changed.

"It's the glucose," she said. "The grape. Glucose plus oxygen, six oxygens, becomes carbon dioxide plus water plus energy. That's the whole equation. That's it."

"That's it? That took you four hours to learn 'eat grape, exhale grape'?"

"Six oxygen molecules," Jessica said, jabbing the paper. "Six CO2, six water. It's exact. It has to balance." She was talking faster now, the way she did when something was actually assembling itself in her head. "The glucose gets broken down, and the part where it actually makes the ATP, the usable energy, happens in the mitochondria. That's what I couldn't hold onto before. It's not a list of vocabulary. It's a route. Glucose comes in, gets taken apart step by step, and the energy ends up as ATP. You can trace it."

Angelie was watching her with an expression Jessica chose to read as skepticism rather than pity. "You said you were basically fine."

"I am basically fine."

"You said that two weeks ago and then you didn't turn in the lab."

Jessica peeled the wet ring off her notes and looked at the clock she'd drawn that morning, a circle with arrows, the route she was supposed to already know for the quiz she'd gotten a D on. She had told herself the D was ancillary, a small thing, one assignment, not the real signal. She had told her mother something similar. She had been very organized about all this telling.

"Do you actually want help, or do you want to keep failing privately?" Angelie said. "Because Petra will quiz you. Petra's annoying about it, but she knows this stuff cold."

"I'll figure it out."

Angelie shrugged and ate another grape, and Jessica watched her breathe, ordinary and unbothered, in and out, and thought about how Angelie's lungs were quietly doing algebra with her lunch and had been doing it all afternoon without either of them noticing. The backyard felt different suddenly, less like scenery and more like a place where an enormous transaction was occurring in every leaf and every lung. She put her finger on the equation again and traced it left to right, glucose to oxygen to carbon dioxide to water, and then she turned the page over and did it backward from memory.

"Watch," she said. "No notes." She wrote it on the dry part of the table in pencil, straight through: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. "Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water. That's it. That's the whole thing."

"Congratulations," Angelie said. "You can do math about my grape."

Jessica laughed before she could decide not to. At the edge of the yard the pond sat still in the late light, and somewhere under that green surface the plants were doing the whole thing in reverse, she supposed, though she couldn't quite see how yet, and she didn't pretend to. She texted Petra: tomorrow, my backyard, bring your notes. Then she picked up the pencil and drew the mitochondrion again, bigger this time, and started the route at the beginning.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false; validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true.
story:
The group chat lit up at 9:47 on a Thursday night, while Joseph sat at the diner counter with his phone propped against the napkin dispenser, waiting for his eggs. Jett had typed: "All dragons are made of igneous rock. Everything made of igneous rock is older than my grandmother. Therefore all dragons are older than my grandmother." Then, a second later: "Valid."

Cora replied before Joseph could. "You can't say valid. There are no dragons. It's like saying all unicorns pay taxes, therefore unicorns file in April. It's just noise."

"It's not noise," Jett typed. "It's valid and you're mad about it."

Joseph set down his fork. Through the window he could see the parking lot going dark, the pumps across the road throwing long yellow light. He typed slowly, thumb hovering. He had taken the logic unit in Mr. Malik's class three weeks ago, and one sentence from the worksheet had stuck to him like a burr, though at the time it had seemed like the driest thing in the unit.

"Wait," he typed. "Jett is using the word right. An argument is valid when it's impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false. That's the whole test. It's about the shape of the thing, not whether the stuff in it is true."

Cora's reply came fast, three dots appearing and vanishing twice before the message landed. "So you're telling me a fake argument can be valid."

"Yes," Joseph typed. "That's exactly what I'm telling you."

He read his own message back and felt a small flare of doubt. He pulled up the worksheet photo he'd taken, scrolled, and found Mr. Malik's line printed in the margin, unhelpfully brief: validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true. So he had remembered it correctly. But remembering a sentence and knowing what to do with it were different projects, and Cora was already typing again.

"Fine, genius. Is this valid: All dragons hoard an annuity. Cora is a dragon. Therefore Cora hoards an annuity."

"Yes," Joseph typed, and then, because it felt incomplete, "and it's valid in exactly the same way as Jett's. If it were somehow true that all dragons hoard an annuity and true that I'm a dragon, the conclusion couldn't be false. That's all the word claims."

"I'm not a dragon, though," Cora typed.

"I know. Neither of us is. The premises are false and the argument is still valid. You're allowed to hate that."

There was a pause long enough that the waitress came and refilled his coffee. He watched the little "typing" bubble pulse and thought about how strange it was that a chain of made-up claims could have a real property. Nobody was lying exactly; Jett hadn't claimed dragons existed. He'd only built a container and shown that nothing could leak out of it. The premises could all be true only in a world where the conclusion was also true, and it seemed almost unfair that the actual world got no vote.

"Okay," Cora typed. "Then what's the point of it? If it doesn't have to be true, why does the word matter?"

Jett answered that one. "Because you can check the shape before you know anything about the world. That's the whole trick. Plug in stuff you don't know yet and see what it would force."

Joseph read that twice. It was better than anything he'd managed, and it opened a question he hadn't considered: whether a form you could trust with unknown contents was more useful or less useful than a claim you could check directly. He started typing a reply, deleted it, started again.

"Here's what I actually think," he typed. "Jett's right about the word and Cora's right to push back. Valid doesn't mean good. A valid argument with false premises tells you nothing about grandmothers or dragons. But it does tell you something about the shape, and the shape is the part that survives. Both things are true at once and neither one absolves the other."

"I hate when you do the both-sides thing," Cora typed, but she added a thumbs-up after, which Joseph had learned to read as partial surrender.

Jett sent a single line: "New rule. Every argument in this chat gets graded. Valid but false, valid and true, invalid but true, invalid and false. Four houses. Like sorting."

"That's actually not a bad system," Cora typed. "Except you invented it, which lowers my confidence in all four houses."

Joseph looked at the eggs cooling on his plate. He was still not certain whether validity was a property of the world or only of the way people talked about the world, and he typed that honestly, adding that he'd ask Mr. Malik tomorrow, not to be told the answer, but to find out whether the question had one. Then he picked up his fork.

Across the table, an old man reading a newspaper glanced over. "You kids arguing about dragons?"

"Sort of," Joseph said. "Mostly about whether the dragons have to be real."

The man turned back to his paper and said, "They never do."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: A 2008 trial in Norway found that young female soccer players aged 13 to 17 who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall.
story:
Lucas arrived at the community pool at six fifty in the morning with a spiral notebook, a pencil he had chewed to splinters, and a plan he did not yet believe in. The swim club's season opener was in nine days, and Coach had announced, with the flatness of someone who had already lost this argument many times, that whoever wanted to could design the team's weekly training program. Lucas had volunteered before he could talk himself out of it, mostly because Zaid had elbowed him and whispered, "You love spreadsheets more than people," which was only half true.

The deadline was Thursday's practice. He had today, Monday, to draft something, and Ms. Teo, the lifeguard who opened the pool and who had once swum competitively in Singapore, had agreed to look it over during her break.

He spread the notebook on the wet concrete beside lane four and wrote Monday: hard set, Tuesday: harder set, Wednesday: hardest set. It looked like progress. It looked like effort. Then Zaid dropped his bag beside Lucas's head, read the page upside down, and said, "Where are the rest days?"

"There's no time for rest days," Lucas said. "The meet is in nine days."

Zaid stretched his hamstrings against the wall, unbothered. "My sister's soccer team does this thing called the FIFA 11+. It's just a warm-up, takes ten minutes. There was a trial in Norway, 2008, girls thirteen to seventeen, and they got about a third fewer injuries overall doing it."

"A third fewer," Lucas repeated, in the tone of someone being sold a time-share.

"Look it up. I don't care. But you're the one writing rest and warm-ups into the plan, and I'm the one who pulled my shoulder last season because we jumped in cold and swam like idiots." Zaid said this cheerfully, the way he said most things, and then he was gone, off to the changing room with a wave that meant no offense taken, none intended.
