Lucas sat with his pencil. He liked training the way he liked math: more input, more output. Rest days felt like a tax on effort, a concession to weakness. But his shoulder still remembered February, that grinding wrongness mid-pull, and how the etiology, according to the physio, had been tediously simple: too much load, too little preparation, too much enthusiasm. Overuse injuries were practically endemic on teams that trained every day without structure, and the physio had said "endemic" with a little shrug, as if describing weather.

Kiptyn arrived at seven fifteen, late as always, hair uncombed, holding a gas station coffee he was too young to have bought himself. "Are you the program guy?" he said. "Everyone's saying there's a program guy."

"I might be the program guy."

"Make Friday easy. Please. I'm begging you. My legs are dead by Friday and then I swim like a manatee." Kiptyn dropped onto the bench and began pulling on his fins with the urgency of a man who had never once been on time for anything. It was hard not to like him. It was impossible to rely on him, which Lucas was beginning to understand were not the same problem.

At Ms. Teo's break, she read the notebook with her chin in her hand. She did not give a speech. She asked one question: "What's the most important day in this plan?" Lucas said Monday, because Monday set the tone. She turned the page toward him and tapped Wednesday, which he had labeled hardest set. "This is where they break," she said. "You've built a machine that grinds." Then she handed it back and drank her tea and talked about the weather in a way that made clear the thinking was his to do.

So he did it, there on the concrete, while the morning swimmers churned up and down the lanes. He crossed out his three ascending days and rebuilt the week: Monday hard, Tuesday moderate with a long technical block, Wednesday off entirely, or as good as off, with mobility work and a ten-minute structured warm-up like the one Zaid's sister's team did, adapted for shoulders instead of knees. Thursday hard again, Friday easy for Kiptyn's sake and everyone else's, Saturday race-pace rehearsal, Sunday rest. He wrote the warm-up at the top of every single day, not because he fully believed ten minutes could matter, but because a third fewer injuries was a third fewer injuries, and a team that lost its swimmers to pulled shoulders in week three had no program at all, only a schedule with ambitions.

What he could not decide, and wrote honestly in the margin because the margin was where he kept his doubts, was whether the Norway numbers, from young female soccer players, meant anything at all for a swim team of mixed, exhausted teenagers. Maybe warm-ups were warm-ups. Maybe water and grass were different worlds. He did not know, and he refused to pretend he did, though he underlined the warm-up line twice anyway, on the theory that being careful probably generalized even when statistics did not.

At Thursday's practice he handed out photocopies, badly stapled, still warm from the machine by the vending machines. Zaid read his, looked up, and said, "Rest day Wednesday. Warm-up every day. Look at you." Kiptyn pointed at Friday and said, "Easy? You beautiful nerd," loud enough that two lanes over, a woman doing breaststroke laughed into the water. Coach read the page for a long moment, tapped the margin where Lucas had written not sure this transfers, but the warm-up is cheap insurance, and said nothing, which Lucas chose to take as approval.

The team did the warm-up that evening on the deck, all fourteen of them, clumsy and half-asleep, Kiptyn doing the shoulder circles with a coffee still in his left hand. Lucas counted them through it, checked the clock, and when the ten minutes were up, watched them jump into the water together, one after another, like something that had been waiting all morning for exactly this.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
The kitchen at Jayde's house smelled like burnt sugar, because someone had left a tray of pecans in the oven too long, and the windows were open to let out the smoke even though it was November. Alexis sat at the counter with Charlotte's essay in front of her, five pages printed and already annotated in pencil, and she kept rearranging the pages the way you shuffle cards when you don't want to play yet. "You've read it twice," Jayde said, leaning on the fridge. "You've read it four times. Just tell her."

"She'll be here in twenty minutes," Alexis said, which was not an answer. The essay was Charlotte's application piece for the student-run literary magazine, the one Alexis co-edited, and it was supposed to be the best thing Charlotte had ever written. It wasn't. It was turgid, thick with clauses stacked on clauses, every simple idea wrapped in three layers of formal dress, and somewhere under all of it was a genuinely good argument about the way their school's small polity of honors students policed its own borders. Alexis could see the good argument. That was the problem. If she couldn't see it, she could just say no.

Jayde pulled out the stool across from her and sat, chin in her hands. "What are you going to say?"

"I practiced in the car. I said, 'The middle section loses momentum.'" Alexis frowned at the pages. "But that's not even true. The whole thing loses momentum. The middle is where it loses it worst."

"So say that."

"You don't say that to Charlotte." She said it more sharply than she meant to, and Jayde's eyebrows went up, and Alexis softened, turning her pencil over and over. "Last year I told her the story she submitted was confusing. One word. Confusing. She didn't submit anything again for eight months." The pencil's hexagon pressed a line into her fingers. She could still remember Charlotte's face doing its quick, polite closing, like a window shutting to keep out weather.

Jayde went to rescue the last of the pecans, sliding the tray out with a dish towel, and blew on one and ate it anyway. "So lie to her."

"No." Alexis laid her hand flat on the pages. "That's the thing. Lying is worse. If I say it's fine and we publish it, everyone who reads the magazine sees it's not fine, and she knows, and she never trusts me again. If I say it's fine and we don't publish it, that's worse, because then there's no reason." Ms. Horváth had told her, when she handed over the editorship, that the job was mostly this: not choosing the pieces, but telling people the truth about the ones that didn't make it. Alexis had thought that sounded easy in September. It was November now.

She had gone to Ms. Horváth that afternoon, actually, hoping to be excused from the whole task, and Ms. Horváth had not excused her. She had gone to her shelf, taken down a folder, and pulled out a single printed page, one study among many, and said only, "Read this tonight. Not before." Alexis had it in her bag now. She took it out and smoothed it on the counter, and Jayde came around to read over her shoulder, still chewing pecans.

It was a study from 2014, led by a researcher named David Yeager. Students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them. Alexis read it twice, and then a third time, and the smoke had cleared but the room still smelled sweet and scorched, and she noticed her own breathing had slowed, like something had lined itself up. "That's it," she said quietly. "That's the missing half." All her practicing in the car had been about softening the criticism, padding it, trying to propitiate Charlotte before the blow. But the study wasn't about softening. The criticism stayed critical. What changed was one sentence of belief added to it, one plain statement that the standard was high and that Charlotte, specifically, could reach it. Not flattery. Belief.

"So you'd say what?" Jayde asked.

"I'd say the essay is overwritten, that the argument about the honors students is buried, that I want it, that I think she can dig it out." Alexis was already writing in the margin of the last page, small letters, not for Charlotte yet, just to see the shape of the words. "The hard part first. Then the sentence." She looked up. "Do you think that's manipulative? Telling someone you believe in them so they'll do what you want?"

Jayde considered it, cracking a pecan in half with her thumbnail. "Do you believe it?"

"That's the strange part," Alexis said. "I do. I keep trying to get out of saying the hard thing because I do." The doorbell rang before Jayde could answer, and they both looked toward the hallway, and Alexis gathered the pages, squared them against the counter, and found that her hands were almost steady. Jayde mouthed, "Hard part first," and pointed at the doorway.

Charlotte came into the kitchen with her coat still on and her own copy of the essay folded under her arm, and she said, "So, is it terrible?" before she'd even sat down, laughing a little, the way people laugh when they've asked the question they most don't want answered.

Alexis slid the pages across the counter toward her, and said, "Parts of it are overwritten. The part that matters isn't."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
The car was the same beige sedan his mother had driven to night shifts for eleven years, and it smelled like her, cough drops and cold coffee, which Mason found both comforting and slightly alarming as he adjusted the seat forward for the first time. His father folded himself into the passenger seat with the patient expression of a man propitiating some household god of teenage milestones, though whether Mason or the car was the god remained unclear. In the back seat, wedged between two laundry baskets, Dexter grinned and said he'd ridden along to supervise the supervision.

"Empty parking lot first," his father said. "Then the loop around the neighborhood if you don't kill us."

"Nobody's killing anybody," Mason said, and turned the key too far, so the starter ground and the engine, already running, complained.

The lot behind the middle school was cracked and puddled from rain the night before, and Mason spent twenty minutes learning that a gas pedal was not a switch. His father kept his right hand hovering near the wheel, never touching it, which Mason understood was a kind of restraint and tried not to resent. Dexter, from behind, offered commentary. "You're riding the brake, bro. Also you're an anachronistic driver, you drive like it's 1950 and everyone's in a hat."

"Everything is an anachronism to you since you got your permit," Mason said, but he eased his foot off the brake.

When they graduated to the street, his father said, "Following distance. Pick a marker, a driveway, a sign, and count when the car ahead passes it. You want three seconds before you reach it."

"Three?" Dexter leaned between the seats. "Two is plenty. I've been doing two since day one, nobody's hit me."

"You've had a license for six weeks," Mason said.

"Three seconds," his father said again, without heat. "And you add a second for each difficulty. It rained last night, so the road's wet. That's four."

Mason counted a mailbox as a minivan somewhere ahead of them passed it. One, two, three, four, and only then did the beige sedan's nose draw level with it. Four seconds felt enormous, a stretch of empty asphalt so long it seemed like a moral position rather than a measurement. He thought of Dexter's two, quick and casual, a city way of thinking, traffic as a negotiation you won by being close. His father's way treated the space ahead as something you owed, whether or not anyone was watching.

The loop took them past the rec center where Dany worked the front desk, and Mason, seeing her through the glass waving with a whole arm, lifted his fingers off the wheel to wave back and immediately drifted toward the curb. His father said his name once, quietly, in the tone that made the name do the work of a paragraph, and Mason corrected. His hands were shaking slightly, not from fear exactly, but from the discovery that a car responds to intentions, that it had been receiving his panic and his pride and his distraction all at once and translating them into motion.

At the stop sign by Ms. Harper's house, she was out on her porch wrapping her fig tree in burlap against the coming frost, an act Mason's father called the right kind of stubborn. She waved them through with a gardening glove. Dexter said, apropos of nothing, that his biology teacher had told him genes aren't destiny, environment shapes everything, and then added, "Though honestly my whole family drives like maniacs, so if there's a driving phenotype, I'm doomed."

"There's no driving phenotype," his father said. "There's a following distance. Watch the road."

Back in the driveway, engine off, Mason sat with his hands still on the wheel and thought about what he actually believed. Dexter's two seconds wasn't stupid; it was a bet that you'd see trouble in time, that closeness was efficiency. His father's three plus one wasn't cowardice; it was a bet that you wouldn't see trouble in time, that the gap was the only honest answer to not knowing. Mason couldn't prove which bet was truer, and he suspected the answer changed depending on the road, the rain, the hour. What he knew was that the four seconds had been the only part of the lesson that had felt like thinking rather than reflex, and that he wanted the version of driving where he got to keep thinking.

"So tomorrow?" he said.

"Tomorrow," his father said, and got out, and stood in the driveway in the cold, waiting for whatever Mason did next.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent killer and is found mainly by measuring it.
story:
Jade had the cuff around her grandfather's arm before he'd finished his second cup of tea, which she considered a small victory, since negotiating with him usually took the length of a cricket match. "Hold still," she said, pumping the bulb. "You're the best practice dummy I've got."

"I am not a dummy," her grandfather said. "I am a volunteer. There is a difference, and it is dignity."

The kitchen smelled of toast and the bitter tea he insisted on, and the late light came through the window at the angle that turned everything jaundiced and gold, even the fridge. Jade watched the needle fall and tried to remember what Ms. Nkosi had drilled into them that afternoon: systolic over diastolic, what the numbers meant, which ones sat in the good range and which ones made a doctor frown. She read the dial twice, wrote the numbers on the back of an envelope, and frowned at them herself.

"Too high?" her grandfather asked, peering at her notes upside down.

"A bit. Maybe." She lowered her voice as though the cuff might overhear. "But I'm new at this, so it could also be that I'm terrible."

"You are not terrible. And anyway, it doesn't matter, because I feel fine." He spread his hands, palms up, a man presenting evidence. "If it were really high, I would feel it. One feels these things. Your grandmother, God rest her, knew when her pressure was up. She'd say, Mkhulu, my head is hot, and she'd be right."

Jade chewed on this. It sounded reasonable, the way things sound reasonable in kitchens. Feelings as instruments. She thought of Ephraim, who trusted nothing he couldn't graph, and of Taya, who trusted her grandmother's opinions on everything from weather to boyfriends, and how each of them would try to subsume the other's whole worldview under their own if you let them. She did not want to do that. She wanted to hold both ideas at once, like carrying two full mugs through a doorway, and see which one spilled.

"You know what we learned today?" she said carefully. "High blood pressure usually doesn't feel like anything."

"Then how would I know I have it?"

"That's the thing. You mostly wouldn't. It doesn't announce itself. It gets found by measuring it. Which is what I'm doing. Right now. To you."

He looked at his own arm, at the cuff, as if it had betrayed a confidence. "That's a terrible design."

"I know."

"A condition with no symptoms. How is a man supposed to manage that?"

"With a cuff," Jade said, "and, apparently, his granddaughter."

He laughed, and she measured him again, and the numbers came out a little lower but still not what the worksheet in her bag would call ideal. She told him what Ms. Nkosi had said about the heart working against narrow, stubborn pipes, and how the things he liked to eat, the salty relish, the tinned everything, could nudge the numbers up over years, and how walking, actual walking, not walking to the car, could nudge them down. She was careful not to lecture. She had watched him walk out of rooms on doctors who lectured.

"So you are saying my fried onions are against me."

"I'm saying they're on the other team."

"And the walking is on my team."

"Small, slow, on your team. Like a very lazy defender."

He nodded and took another sip of his terrible tea, and Jade saw that he was not dismissing her; he was turning it over, the way he turned over a chess move, testing whether it would hold. "When I was a boy," he said, "we walked everywhere because there was no other way. Now I drive to the shop that is four hundred metres away. I will grant you this looks bad on paper."

"It does look bad on paper," she agreed. "It's practically a deposition against you."

The word made him snort into his tea. "Write it down, then. Testimony of the accused: guilty of driving to the corner shop."

She wrote it on the envelope, under the numbers, and then, because it was true and he deserved to have it said plainly, she added that she wasn't certain how much any of it mattered for him specifically. She was seventeen with a borrowed cuff and one afternoon of instruction. The numbers could be off because she'd rushed, or because he'd been arguing, or because the machine in the clinic would tell a different story entirely. "I don't want you scared," she said. "I want you measured. Properly. Will you come to the clinic with me Saturday?"

He was quiet for a moment, tapping the envelope against the table. "If I come," he said, "we walk there."

"It's two kilometres."

"I know how far it is. I'm starting my defence."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, like red and green, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter.
story:
Stella had taped the print of Frida Kahlo's self-portrait above her desk with two strips of masking tape, which her mother called vandalism, and now she was supposed to write eight hundred words about it for Mr. Qureshi, who had specifically banned the phrase "this painting is beautiful because."

"It's not a compliment assignment," he had said. "It's formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Tell me what the painting does, not what it does to your heart."

Stella's heart, meanwhile, was doing nothing helpful. It was eleven days until the essay deadline and three days until her sister's wedding shower, for which their mother expected Stella to assemble two hundred favours shaped like swans. The swans sat in boxes by her bed like unfinished thoughts.

Koraly came over after school, dropped her bag on the swans, and looked at the print. "Why is her face so calm when there's blood all over her neck?"

"That's what I have to figure out. Calm versus horror. Green background, red beads." Stella leaned closer. The necklace of thorns dripped red drops onto Kahlo's white shirt, and behind everything a wall of green leaves. The reds and the greens seemed almost to vibrate where they touched.

"Is that a thing," Koraly said, "or is your eye tired?"

Stella dug out her art notes from first semester. She turned pages past colour wheels until she found the diagram, the circle her old teacher had drawn with red opposite green, yellow opposite purple. Complementary colours, the margin said in Stella's own handwriting, sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter. She read it twice. So the vibration was real, a fact with a name, not a hallucination induced by swan folding.

"Complementary colours," she said out loud, mostly to hear it.

"Congratulations," Koraly said. "Now you have one paragraph."

One paragraph was not eight hundred, and by Thursday Stella had one paragraph and a hundred and forty swans. Lexie texted her a photo of her own essay outline, colour-coded, and Stella put the phone face down and stared at the painting. Kahlo had put herself in the exact centre, frontal and unmoving, like something from antiquity staring out of stone, while the leaves crowded in and the hummingbird hung dead at her throat. The stillness at the middle, the riot around it. Stella wrote: the composition holds a fixed centre inside an unstable field. Then she crossed out "field" as pretentious, then wrote it again, because it was accurate, and accuracy was the whole religion of this assignment.

The symbolism was where she got stuck. The thorn necklace, the dead hummingbird, the panther cub on her shoulder and the monkey. Lexie said the monkey was clearly an ex-boyfriend. Koraly said the monkey was capitalism. Mr. Qureshi had warned them against decoding symbols like a vending machine, one meaning per slot, and Stella suspected that any essay claiming to know what Kahlo meant would be a lie, and also that an essay admitting total ignorance would be a failure. Somewhere between certainty and surrender there was a position she could actually defend.

She tried writing it both ways. In the first version, the thorns meant suffering and the hummingbird meant freedom, dead. In the second, she wrote that the symbols refused to settle, that Kahlo's animals watched her with the same calm she wore, and that the painting's meaning might be precisely that composure, the composed face wearing pain like a necklace. Then she looked at that sentence and thought it was actually good, which frightened her a little, because usually when she thought that, Mr. Qureshi did not.

On Saturday, with the swans finally done and the shower finally over, she sat at her desk and reread the whole draft. The complementary colour paragraph felt solid now: red and green opposite each other on the colour wheel, and side by side they made each other brighter, which was why the blood and the leaves intensified each other, why calm and horror sharpened each other too. Whether Kahlo intended that resonance or simply felt her way to it, Stella could not know, and she wrote that she could not know, and decided that leaving it open was more honest than inventing a motive for a dead painter. Some claims, she wrote, exceed the evidence, and this essay would not make them. She underlined nothing. It felt exhilarating, actually, to argue for uncertainty instead of papering over it, though she doubted Mr. Qureshi would put it that way.

Her mother came in without knocking, holding a leftover swan. "You've been at that desk all weekend. Is this germane to your future?"

"It's due Monday," Stella said.

"That's not what I asked."

Stella saved the file, closed the laptop, and took the swan from her mother's hand. It was lopsided, like all of them. "It's Kahlo," she said. "The one with the thorns." Her mother set it back on the box by the bed and left the door open behind her, and Stella looked up one more time at the green leaves, the red drops, the face at the centre holding still.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
story:
The gown was already too hot by the time Aiden crossed the parking lot, its synthetic fabric catching on the door handle of his mother's car. He had come back after the ceremony to find the sunglasses he'd left on the dashboard, and now he stood there in the emptying lot holding the leather folder the school had given him, the one with his name stamped in gold. Kabir was leaning against a light pole a few spaces away, still in his gown, eating fries out of a paper tray as though graduation were an inconvenient lunch break.

"You're not even going to look at it?" Kabir called over. "Two weeks of exams for that thing and you won't open it."

Aiden thumbed the folder's edge. He had been putting it off all afternoon, half because it felt ceremonial and half because he suspected the ceremony was mostly cardboard. When he finally opened it, the paper inside lay flat, unfolded, printed once, sealed in plastic. He held it up to the light between two parked cars. "It's not even folded," he said. "You'd think, for the money they spent on the folder, they could at least fold the paper."

Angel appeared from behind a minivan, cap in hand, dragging her tassel through her fingers like a worry stone. "What are you two doing standing out here in the sun?" She looked at the diploma, then at Aiden, and something in her expression said she knew something. "You know why it's called a diploma? Because it comes from a Greek word meaning paper folded double. They used to fold official documents, back whenever."

"Paper folded double," Aiden repeated. He looked at the folder again, at the crease down its spine where the leather had been folded over itself to make the cover, and then at the flat certificate. "So the folder is the honest part and the paper is the fake part. Or maybe the other way around." He wasn't sure which was funnier, or which was sadder, and he found he wanted to sit with the question rather than settle it.

Ms. Lau was stacking chairs by the gym entrance, and when she saw the three of them she waved them over, belligerent in the heat the way only a teacher on her last duty of the year could be, telling the custodian exactly where every chair belonged. Aiden asked her whether Angel was right about the Greek. She said she believed so, but that Aiden should check, which was what Ms. Lau said about everything, including things she had taught for twenty years. He looked it up on his phone, standing between a station wagon and a convertible with a sunshade in the windshield, and read the line twice.

"It's true," he said. "Paper folded double, from folding official documents." He turned the fact over the way he'd turned over problems in Ms. Lau's class, where she had a habit of calling a variable a confounder when it disguised what was really going on. He wondered whether the diploma was a confounder in its own ceremony. Everyone had acted as though the folder were the achievement, when the achievement was four years of mornings, of essays and dropped passes and the winter Kabir stopped speaking to him for a month and then started again as if nothing had happened. The paper couldn't suture those years together, and neither could the folding, but at least the folding had once admitted that a document needed to be closed, protected, opened deliberately.

"My dad says nobody ever asks to see it," Kabir said, balling up the fry tray. "Not for jobs, not for anything. It just goes in a drawer."

"My mom put hers on the wall," Angel said. "Above the toilet."

They laughed, and then didn't, and the lot was emptying in the long afternoon light, gowns coming off over T-shirts, cars backing out one by one. Aiden tried to hold two thoughts at once without forcing them into one: that the folder was a costume and the paper was a prop, and that he was still, undeniably, different from what he'd been in September, and that neither thought canceled the other out. He couldn't make them fit together, and he decided, cautiously, that maybe he didn't have to yet. That felt less like giving up than like leaving a page unfolded on purpose.

He closed the folder, then opened it again and folded the diploma in half, carefully, along no particular line, so the crest broke at the crease. Angel said, "You're going to ruin it." Kabir said nothing, just watched, chewing.

"It's the only honest version," Aiden said, and put it in the car, folded double, on the dashboard next to his sunglasses.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.
story:
Eva had the kitchen table to herself, which meant the laptop, three library books, and a mug gone cold all belonged to her until dinner. The paper was due in nine days, and it was supposed to be an argument, not a report, which was the part that kept tripping her. She had chosen street trees, the way a lined boulevard could cool a block in summer, and she had found a perfect paragraph in the second book that said almost exactly what she wanted to say. So she typed it in her own words, changed "canopy" to "cover of leaves," reordered the sentences, and felt the small satisfaction of a section finished.

Van arrived at four with a backpack she didn't take off, which meant she wasn't staying long, or meant she wanted Eva to ask why she was there at all. Van's want was simple and long-standing: she had left her own paper until the last possible week, and Eva's habit of starting early had rescued her before. She dropped into the chair across the table and pulled the nearest book toward her without asking.

"Is this one good?"

"It's the one with the cooling data," Eva said. "There's a chapter on block temperature." She slid her laptop half toward Van to show the outline, and that was when she saw the paragraph again, sitting there in her own phrasing, no footnote under it, nothing in the bibliography yet. She'd meant to come back to it. Probably she'd meant to.

"You're already at three pages?" Van said. "Eva. I have a title and a topic sentence and a bag of chips."

"Start with the arboreal canopy stuff, it's the easiest to summarize." Eva pulled the laptop back, but slowly, because something about the paragraph was bothering her and she hadn't yet named what.

The trouble was that it didn't feel like copying. She had rewritten it, genuinely; not a single sentence matched the original. In the classes before this one, rewriting had been the whole point, the thing teachers asked for as proof you hadn't cheated. There was a memory underneath that belief, from eighth grade, when Mr. Campbell-Brown, who had been her neighbor long before he was her teacher, had sat on her porch steps and told her that a fact she'd found in an encyclopedia needed to be credited in her poster about owls. She'd been indignant, she remembered, because she'd written it in her own words, and he'd only laughed and said the encyclopedia would survive. She had forgotten the lesson and kept the indignation, apparently, for four years.

Mr. Campbell-Brown was still the neighbor. His porch light came on at five, every evening, regular as a bell, and Eva found herself watching it while Van talked about how she might do her whole paper in one marathon Thursday. The synchronicity of the light and her thought gave her a small, superstitious chill, as though the evening were agreeing with her that she should go ask him something. She didn't want to. She wanted to finish the section.

What she did instead, because Van was watching and because finishing would have felt like slamming a door, was walk across the frost-stiff grass and knock. He had the same style handbook on his shelf that the class used, and he took it down without a word of commentary, which was his way, and let her stand in his doorway while she found the page.

She found it. The sentence sat in the middle of a section on academic honesty, plain as a stop sign: putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording. She read it twice. Her paragraph on the cooling effect was someone else's finding, someone else's years of measurement, and she had dressed it in her own sentences and let it walk out the door unaccounted for.

"That's me," she said, mostly to the handbook. "That's literally my paragraph."

"Mm," said Mr. Campbell-Brown, and went back to his crossword, because he never explained anything when you could read it yourself.

Back in her kitchen, Van had not started her paper; she had started a list of reasons she couldn't start it, which was its own kind of document. But Eva's mind was on the laptop, and on a detail she had been keeping at arm's length all afternoon: the draft had already gone out. She had emailed it to the teacher two nights ago for feedback, unfootnoted, unrepentant, with the borrowed idea sitting in her own words in the middle of page two. That was the fact she'd been not-naming, and now it was named, and there was nothing to do but open her email.

The reply had come while she'd been across the street. She stood over the laptop with her coat still on and Van saying something about marathon Thursdays in the background, and she made herself click it.

The comment on page two said only: "Interesting claim. Where does it come from?" No accusation, no tone, just the question, which was somehow worse, because it was the exact question she couldn't answer without admitting she'd nearly taken something without paying.

She sat down and opened the second book to the page with the paragraph and began building the footnote, typing the author's name, the title, the city, the year, following the handbook down on the table beside her. Van leaned over the divider of books.

"Eva, is that a citation? You cite yourself now?"

"It's not mine," Eva said. "That's the whole thing. It never was."

Van looked at the screen, then at the book, then at her own nearly empty notebook, and something in her face rearranged itself, a slow, reluctant arithmetic. She reached over and picked up the handbook.

"Can I borrow this?" Van said.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Larger samples give more precise estimates, so a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one.
story:
Sierra spread the two articles across the library table an hour before the writing club deadline, because Mr. Oyelaran wanted every critical review handed to him by eight o'clock, typed, before the room closed. The first article, from a small psychology journal, surveyed thirty college students and found that most of them preferred handwritten notes to typed ones. The second, from a much larger journal, surveyed thirty thousand students across several countries and reported almost the same proportion. Her draft said the two studies "agree, which strengthens the conclusion," and she had been proud of that sentence all week.

Eliam dropped his backpack on the chair beside her and read over her shoulder without asking. "You treat them like they're the same thing."

"They found the same thing. Ninety percent of one, eighty-eight percent of the other. That's agreement."

"Okay, but which one would you trust?"

She said both, obviously, and he pulled the second article toward himself and tapped the methods section. Sierra reached for the first article to check its numbers again, and while she did, Ryker arrived with the club's submission forms and the news that Mr. Oyelaran had called the choice of which review to feature in the school journal "a plebiscite," meaning the whole club would vote at eight, so whatever she wrote had to be finished before then. Ryker was laconic about it, as he was about most things: "Vote at eight. Be done." Sierra looked at the two sample sizes printed in front of her, thirty and thirty thousand, and felt something shift in her argument, though she could not yet say what.

She read her own sentence again. If ninety percent of thirty students preferred handwriting, that was twenty-seven people; three people changing their minds would swing it to eighty percent. The same result from thirty thousand students could not be moved by three people, or by three hundred. A result from a small study, she wrote in the margin, carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one, and the word "same" was the part she had been ignoring. The two articles agreed, but they were not equal evidence. Her draft had praised the agreement without asking what it rested on, and there was an hour to fix it.

Eliam watched her cross out the sentence she had been proud of, and he understood that she had arrived somewhere without his pushing her the last step. He had argued with her because arguing was how they worked, not because he wanted her to lose; in the fourth grade they had fought about whether a whale could beat a shark and had ended up checking out the same library book, one name on the card after the other. Now she wrote fast, pen moving before typing, and he read the new paragraph as she finished it: that a careful review had to weigh how much weight each study could bear, and that the smaller study was suggestive while the larger was decisive, and that this difference, not the similarity, was the real story.

"Read it out," he said. "You'll hear what's wrong."

She read it aloud. The sentence about margins was fine. The next sentence used "proves" three times, and Mr. Oyelaran circled that word in red on every draft he returned, so she cut two of the three and changed the last one to "suggests." Ryker, filling in the submission form across the table, asked which article she was backing, and she said both, but not evenly, and he wrote that down as her answer.

At eight o'clock Mr. Oyelaran came in with his mug and collected the pages one by one. He read Sierra's review standing by the window, and Eliam watched his face for the verdict and got nothing, because Mr. Oyelaran's face while grading was a locked door. He set the page down and asked the room, "All in favor of featuring the review of the two note-taking studies?"

Hands went up, more than Eliam expected, maybe because the club had argued about handwriting in September and everyone had opinions. Sierra's hand was up too. He looked at her and saw she was rereading her own last paragraph, mouthing the words, the part where she had written that some questions still could not be settled by either study, such as why students preferred what they preferred.

"You didn't pick a side," Eliam said to her, quietly, while the next review was announced.

"I picked a side about the evidence. The rest I don't know yet." She squared the pages on the table, and after the vote was counted she slid the articles into her folder, the small one on top, and carried both home.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
The ticket machine outside the theater kept rejecting Maika's card, twice, and she was still feeding it in a third time when Amine arrived, holding two drinks he had bought without asking her what she wanted. She noticed this and filed it somewhere, the way she filed most things, without deciding yet whether it was thoughtfulness or presumption. "I got you lemonade," he said. "Guessing."

The film was one neither of them had heard of before Tuesday, a documentary about deep sea vents that Ms. Thompson had recommended to the whole biology class with the warning that it was slow and beautiful and would probably bore half of them. Maika had liked the sound of that. Amine had said sure without enthusiasm, and she had spent the walk to the theater trying to work out whether his flatness was nerves or indifference, and whether those were even different things in a person you didn't know yet.

They found their seats in the middle of the row, the awkward middle where you can't stretch your legs. Amine set both cups in the shared cupholder because there was only one, and Maika watched him do it, watched the two cups wedged together like the evening itself, unstable, dependent on neither of them reaching for a drink at the wrong moment. She had a habit of watching social situations as if they were experiments. Her mother called this her laboratory brain and said it would make her lonely. Her mother also said it would make her a good scientist, so Maika had learned to hold both opinions in her hands at once, like sedimentary layers of the same rock, without needing either to be the true one.

The trailers were still running when Amine reached for his drink. Whether the cup was too full or his elbow caught the armrest, she would never be able to reconstruct. The cup tipped, and cola went across the armrest and into his lap, a dark spreading stain, and the ice clattered down between the seats where it would lie melting for the next two hours. Amine stood up in the dark like a man betrayed by his own body. "Great," he said. "That's great. This is ruined."

People turned. He whispered an apology to the row, to her, to the screen, and went out to the lobby, and Maika sat alone with the lemonade and the melting ice and the sense of a small catastrophe radiating outward. Here was the thing she kept doing to herself, and she knew she did it: she could not simply feel awkward. She had to pathologize it, take it apart, ask what the awkwardness was for, whether it had a function. She sat in the blue projector light and let herself fall into a brief reverie, not about Amine but about a paragraph she had read three weeks ago in a used psychology book from the thrift store, the kind of book with someone else's marginalia in it.

The paragraph had described an experiment from 1966. Elliot Aronson and his colleagues had staged a quiz contestant, highly competent, winning everything, and then, in one version, the contestant knocked over a cup of coffee. Afterward, people rated that contestant as more likable. The book had a name for it, printed in bold, and Maika remembered copying the name into her notebook because it sounded like a spell. The competent person who errs becomes warmer, more human, easier to like. The flawless one stays impressive and stays distant. She had underlined it twice and thought, at the time, that it was probably true, and then thought, in the next moment, that wanting it to be true was not the same as it being true.

Amine came back with wet spots on his jeans where he had tried to rinse them. He slid past their row's knees, sat down, and put his head slightly in his hands. "I'm sorry," he said. "You should just go home. This is the worst first date in history." The documentary was beginning, columns of black water and impossible fish, and Maika leaned toward him so the whole theater wouldn't hear.

"It's called the pratfall effect," she said. "Aronson, 1966. A quiz contestant, really good at the quiz, spills a cup of coffee, and people rated him more likable afterward than the version who never spilled anything."

Amine looked at her. "You made that up to make me feel better."

"I read it in a book with coffee stains on the cover, which I choose to find meaningful." She handed him the lemonade. "You were doing fine before the spill. Now, according to a dead psychologist, you're doing better than fine. Statistically."

"Statistically," he said, and she could hear the smile arrive in his voice before she could see it in the dark. "You keep statistics on this?"

"On everything. It's a problem. My mother says so." The vents on the screen breathed sulfur into the abyss, and fish no one had named until 1977 drifted past like rumors of fish. Amine drank her lemonade without asking, which she filed again, and this time the filing felt warmer, or she let it.

She watched him more than the film, after that. She watched him lean forward at the tube worms, watched him whisper "how" at the pressure numbers, watched him forget the stain entirely. And underneath the watching, a quieter question kept its seat beside her: whether the pratfall effect was really why she felt easier now, or whether she had used a fact the way people use facts, as permission for a feeling they already had. She did not know. She held the question and the lemonade and did not resolve either.

When the lights came up, Amine stood first and offered his hand, and the sticky armrest came away with him, the cupholder's plastic lip clinging to his sleeve like a small stubborn joke, and Maika laughed before she could stop herself.

"See?" he said. "Statistically."

fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The parking lot had filled by noon, though kickoff was still three hours off, and Noah's father had already claimed their section of bleachers with a blanket and a thermos, the way he had every Army-Navy game since Noah was seven. Around them the stadium swelled with gray wool coats and gold braid, midshipmen and cadets chanting at each other across the aisle like rival congregations.

Elsie and Khadija arrived at halftime, squeezing past knees with a bag of soft pretzels they'd smuggled in under Khadija's enormous scarf. Elsie sat down hard beside Noah, breathless. "Tell me you saw that fumble recovery. The whole stadium's fighting about it."

"Nobody can agree on what happened," Khadija said. "The guys in front of us think Navy stripped the ball before his knee was down. My uncle's ready to fight a colonel about it."

Noah had seen it, sort of, from behind a pillar while someone spilled soda down his sleeve. A pile of bodies, an arm swinging out with the ball, a whistle. The referee had pointed Army's way. Half the stadium roared, and the other half went quiet the way crowds do when they are deciding whether to believe an insult.

"There should be a replay," Elsie said, jabbing a finger at the jumbotron, which was showing a live eagle and a corporate logo. "They have the cameras. Why won't they just show it again?"

"That's not how it works here," Noah said, though he realized, saying it, that he didn't actually know how it worked. His father leaned over the blanket and offered the thermos, which was his way of joining a conversation.

"Television does what television wants," his father said. "And what television wants is whatever CBS did in sixty-three."

Noah blinked at him. "What happened in sixty-three?"

"You're the one with the phone," his father said, and settled back, as though the matter were closed. This was the whole of his pedagogy: the fact pointed at, never handed over. Noah resented it and, secretly, relied on it, because his father's facts always turned out to be true, which meant the burden of finding them fell entirely on Noah, and the finding stuck.

He searched it out while the teams changed ends, phone cupped against the wind coming off the field. December 7, 1963, Army-Navy game, same rivalry, older stadium. The first instant replay on television, shown by CBS, using a system devised by a director named Tony Verna. Before that day, a play happened once and then it was gone, and the whole country had argued in the dark. After it, you could see it again, and again, until seeing replaced remembering and everyone agreed, or agreed to pretend they agreed.

"So?" Elsie demanded. The third quarter was starting and the argument around them had curdled into belligerent muttering; the man behind them had begun narrating the disputed play to anyone who would listen, each retelling more favorable to Navy.

"So it's the same game," Noah said. "Army-Navy. Nineteen sixty-three, CBS showed the first instant replay ever, on television, and the guy who figured out how, the director, was Tony Verna. That's the whole reason replays exist." He looked up at the screen still showing the eagle. "But we're here, not watching it on television. The stadium is the one place you don't get the thing your grandpa invented the replay for."

Khadija frowned at the scoreboard clock, which was already bleeding minutes they would need for the walk out. "We have until the end of the quarter before my uncle leaves without us, deadline firm. Do we stay or do we go find a television?"

"That's choosing to watch the game on TV instead of at the game," Elsie said slowly, as if testing whether the sentence could hold that much weight. The teams lined up. Somewhere below them, the play clock wound down, and twenty-two men about to collide were also, for three of them, the answer to whether they'd get home dry.

Noah thought about Verna again, and about his father's closed eyes, and about the way the crowd had already begun to internalize its own versions of the fumble, each side certain, both sides sincere. Maybe the replay wouldn't settle anything; maybe it would only give the argument better lighting. Maybe that was still worth something. He would not pretend to know which. What he knew was that the clock was running and Khadija's uncle was already standing, cracking his knuckles at the exit, and the next snap was two seconds away.

"Go," Noah said, and grabbed Elsie's sleeve. They poured down the stairway with the play unfolding behind their backs, the roar arriving a half beat after the hit, unexplained and unglimpsed, and they burst out into the cold lot where a stranger's van door hung open and a small screen glowed. On it, a pile of bodies, an arm swinging out with the ball, and a whistle, frozen, then again. The man beside the van squinted and said, "Knee was down."
